MOHRE recognises 13 distinct work permit types including standard (mainland), free zone, mission, part-time, temporary, and permits for Golden and Green Visa holders.
rows.evidence_quote: MoHRE has 13 types of work permits. It issues the permits to establishments registered with them, depending on the nature of the job.

rows.fact_text: Total employer cost for sponsoring a new employee visa in the UAE ranges approximately AED 3,000–7,000, covering: Entry Permit (AED 200–500), medical examination (AED 250–350), Emirates ID (AED 270–370, at AED 100/year of visa), residence visa stamping (AED 500–1,000), work permit (AED 300–500), typing/service fees (AED 200–500), and mandatory health insurance (variable). Employers are prohibited from charging employees for any visa costs.
rows.evidence_quote: Costs vary by employee nationality, company category, and free zone. Total 3,000–7,000 AED.

rows.fact_text: To sponsor employees, a UAE employer must: hold a valid and active Trade Licence; be registered with MOHRE; have no labour law violations; demonstrate financial stability to pay wages; comply with employee quota limits; and be enrolled in the Wage Protection System (WPS). Employers must provide health insurance before the visa is issued.
rows.evidence_quote: To sponsor employees, employers must: Valid Trade License: Active and current. MOHRE Registration: Registered establishment. No Violations: Clean labor law compliance record.

rows.fact_text: Employee documents required for UAE employment visa: valid passport with minimum 6 months' validity; passport-sized photographs (white background); educational certificates (attested if required by occupation); professional certificates where applicable; previous employment letters if applicable. Educational certificate attestation chain: Home country Ministry of Education → Home country Ministry of Foreign Affairs → UAE Embassy in home country → UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
rows.evidence_quote: Educational certificates may need attestation from: Home country Ministry of Education, Home country Ministry of Foreign Affairs, UAE Embassy in home country, UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

rows.fact_text: Total UAE employment visa processing takes approximately 2–6 weeks: Initial MOHRE approval (Entry Permit) 1–5 business days; employee travel up to 60 days window; medical fitness test 2–5 business days; Emirates ID 7–14 business days; residence visa stamping 1–3 business days.
rows.evidence_quote: Total 2–6 weeks. Initial approval 1–5 days. Employee travel up to 60 days. Medical test 2–5 days. Emirates ID 7–14 days. Visa stamping 1–3 days.

rows.fact_text: Investors qualify for a 10-year Golden Visa with a minimum capital of AED 2 million in public investments or real estate. Alternatively, property ownership worth AED 2 million or contribution to an establishment paying at least AED 250,000 annually in taxes qualifies. Real estate investments yield a 5-year Golden Visa.
rows.evidence_quote: Minimum capital of AED 2 million; property ownership or contribution to an establishment paying at least AED 250,000 annually in taxes.

rows.fact_text: Entrepreneurs qualify for a 5-year Golden Visa with proof of an innovative or technical project, documentation proving project value, and a letter from a business incubator or relevant authority in the emirate. Successful entrepreneurs with a previously exited business may also qualify.
rows.evidence_quote: Entrepreneurs 5 years: Proof of innovative or technical projects, documents proving project value, letter from a business incubator or relevant authority in the emirate.

rows.fact_text: Highly skilled professionals qualify for a 10-year Golden Visa with a minimum gross salary of AED 30,000 per month (basic salary must be at least 50% of gross). Minimum 2 years with the same employer and a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the employer are also required. Eligible professions include doctors, engineers, scientists, executives, and specialists in priority fields.
rows.evidence_quote: Applicants needed to evidence a minimum gross salary of AED 30,000 (approximately USD 8,169) per month... basic salary of 50% of the total compensation.

rows.fact_text: Scientists and researchers qualify for a 10-year Golden Visa. Requirements through GDRFA include: nomination letter from the UAE Scientists Council; minimum monthly salary of AED 30,000. For Abu Dhabi, applicants need a Master's or PhD degree in Engineering, Technology, Life Sciences or Natural Sciences, and an H-index of 10 or higher (from scientific research).
rows.evidence_quote: The salary must not be less than a monthly salary of approximately AED 30,000 or its equivalent in foreign currencies.

rows.fact_text: Outstanding students qualify for a 5-year Golden Visa (high school achievers) or 10-year Golden Visa (top university students). Requirements include certificates of excellence and recommendation letters from school or university. Students who graduate from top 100 global universities with a GPA of 3.75 or above from UAE universities may qualify.
rows.evidence_quote: Outstanding students: 5 years for high school achievers. 10 years for top university students. Certificates of excellence, recommendation letters from school or university.

rows.fact_text: Golden Visa holders enjoy: long-term renewable residence (5 or 10 years); no requirement for employer sponsorship; ability to stay outside UAE for more than the usual 6-month limit without losing residency; ability to sponsor family members including spouse and children indefinitely; no minimum salary requirement to sponsor family; access to UAE's banking, business, and education ecosystem.
rows.evidence_quote: A long-term, renewable residence visa valid for 5 or 10 years; the privilege of not needing a sponsor; the ability to stay outside the UAE for more than the usual period of six months needed to keep their residence visa valid; the ability to sponsor family members, including spouses and children.

rows.fact_text: Skilled employees qualify for the 5-year Green Visa with: minimum monthly salary of AED 15,000; a valid UAE employment contract; a bachelor's degree or equivalent qualification; and occupational classification at levels 1, 2, or 3 as per MOHRE's occupational classification. No employer sponsorship is required — the visa is self-sponsored.
rows.evidence_quote: The minimum level of education should be a bachelor's degree or equivalent. The salary must be at least 15,000 thousand Dirhams or the equivalent in other currencies.

rows.fact_text: Freelancers qualify for the 5-year Green Visa with minimum annual income of AED 360,000 (approximately AED 30,000/month) or equivalent from freelance activity. A freelance permit from a UAE authority is required. No employer sponsor needed.
rows.evidence_quote: Eligibility varies, including a minimum AED 15,000 monthly salary or AED 360,000 annual freelance income.

rows.fact_text: Green Visa benefits: 5-year self-sponsored residency with no employer needed; can sponsor family members (spouse and children); 90-day grace period after job loss to find new employment or transition; more employment flexibility compared to standard visa; entry permit valid for 60 days to complete residence procedures. Application fee: AED 200 plus VAT (5%).
rows.evidence_quote: Work visa fee: AED200 In addition to the value-added tax (5%). The foreigner is granted a work entry visa under the category of (high-level skilled worker), which permits the holder to remain in the country for (60) sixty days.

rows.fact_text: The UAE Virtual Work (Digital Nomad) Visa requires: employment or self-employment for a company/entity based outside the UAE (work performed remotely); minimum monthly income of USD 3,500 or equivalent in any currency; valid health insurance; and a passport with minimum 6 months' validity. The visa is valid for 1 year, renewable.
rows.evidence_quote: Submit proof that he has a monthly income of no less than (3,500) US dollars or the equivalent in foreign currencies. Submit a valid health insurance document.

rows.fact_text: Virtual Work Visa entry fee: AED 200 plus 5% VAT. If applying from inside the UAE: additional Knowledge Dirham (AED 10), Innovation Dirham (AED 10), and inside-country fee (AED 500). If applying from outside Dubai: total base fees as of August 2024 approximately USD 101 (AED 372.50) including VAT. Processing time: 48 hours via digital channel.
rows.evidence_quote: Virtual work visa fee: AED200 Dirhams. Plus VAT (5%). Additional fees (if the sponsored person is inside the country): Knowledge Dirham: AED10, Innovation Dirham: AED10, Fee inside the country: AED500.

rows.fact_text: Virtual Work Visa holders can sponsor family members (spouse and children) for the same 1-year duration. The visa is renewable annually. No UAE employer sponsorship is required.
rows.evidence_quote: The virtual work has a one-year, extendable period of residence from the date of issuance. For the same period, he can sponsor his family.

rows.fact_text: To sponsor a spouse and children for UAE Family Residence Visa, the sponsor must earn a minimum of AED 4,000 per month, or AED 3,000 per month if employer-provided accommodation is included. Sponsoring parents requires a higher threshold of approximately AED 20,000 per month.
rows.evidence_quote: Financial solvency must be demonstrated, with a minimum monthly income of AED 3,000 plus employer-provided housing, or AED 4,000 if housing is not provided.

rows.fact_text: UAE Family Residence Visa age rules: Dependent sons can be sponsored up to age 25 (previously 18, raised in recent reforms); dependent daughters can be sponsored regardless of age until marriage; male students over 25 can remain on parent's sponsorship if they provide proof of university enrollment at a UAE institution.
rows.evidence_quote: Expatriate residents can sponsor their male child/children up to the age of 25. Male students over the age of 25 can stay on their parents' sponsorship if they provide evidence of attending a higher educational institute. Expatriate residents may continue to sponsor their female children for study, regardless of their age, until she is married.

rows.fact_text: Documents required for UAE Family Residence Visa sponsorship: sponsor's valid residence visa and Emirates ID; sponsor's salary certificate or employment letter; marriage certificate (attested) for spouse; birth certificates (attested) for children; passport copies of all dependants (minimum 6 months' validity); personal photographs; and health insurance for dependants.
rows.evidence_quote: Visa Type: Standard Employment. Minimum Salary: AED 4,000/month. Can Sponsor: Spouse, children, parents.

rows.fact_text: UAE Student Residence Visa is available to international students enrolled full-time at an accredited UAE university or college. The visa is sponsored either by the educational institution or by a resident parent. Requires: certificate from the university specifying study duration; valid passport (6+ months); passport photographs; medical fitness examination; and tuition fee payment confirmation.
rows.evidence_quote: To apply for a student visa, you must submit a certificate issued by the university or institute specifying the duration of the study and meet other general provisions.

rows.fact_text: UAE Student Residence Visa is initially issued for one year and must be renewed annually for the duration of the study programme. High-performing students may qualify for the Golden Visa (10-year). Processing time is typically 3–6 weeks. Renewal should be initiated at least 45 days before expiry.
rows.evidence_quote: Standard student visas are valid for one year and are renewed annually until you complete your program.

rows.fact_text: Emirates ID application process: (1) Obtain or be in process of obtaining UAE residence visa; (2) Submit Emirates ID application via ICP Smart Services website/app or an ICP-accredited typing centre; (3) Attach required documents (passport, visa, photo) — linkage to government databases may auto-populate some fields; (4) Pay fees (AED 100 per year of visa validity + AED 100 smart service fee); (5) Attend biometric appointment at ICP service centre for fingerprints and signature (mandatory for those aged 15+); (6) Receive card via authorised courier (standard) or collect at ICP centre (urgent).
rows.evidence_quote: Individuals who have completed 15 years of age are required to complete the fingerprint and signature procedures through the Authority's service centers. The new Identity Card is delivered through the authorized courier for the standard service, and collected from the Authority's centers for the urgent service.

rows.fact_text: Emirates ID fees for residents: AED 100 per year of visa validity (e.g., 3-year visa = AED 300 for card) plus AED 100 smart service fee. Urgent service: additional AED 150. Standard processing time: 7–10 business days. Emirates ID is mandatory for all UAE residents and required for banking, healthcare, driving licence, SIM card registration, and all government services.
rows.evidence_quote: Fees for issuing a new Identity Card for residents, per year of residence — 100 AED. Smart Service Fees — 100 AED. Urgent service fees (available only at the Authority's service centers) — 150 AED.

rows.fact_text: Emirates ID serves as the sole mandatory identity document for all UAE residents. It is required for: opening bank accounts; obtaining a SIM card (mobile number registration); applying for a driving licence; accessing government services; healthcare registration; school/university enrollment; and property/tenancy (Ejari) registration. Carrying the Emirates ID at all times is legally required.
rows.evidence_quote: The service is mandatory with a passport valid for at least 3 months and proof of residency in the UAE as per the specified categories.

rows.fact_text: Dubai Law No. 11 of 2013 (Health Insurance Law) requires all residents of Dubai — including expatriate employees — to hold valid health insurance meeting or exceeding the minimum Essential Benefits Plan (EBP). Employers must provide and fund health insurance for their employees and are prohibited from asking employees to contribute to the cost of obtaining or renewing the required health insurance.
rows.evidence_quote: The Health Insurance Law of Dubai No 11 of 2013 requires that all Residents must have a level of health insurance that meets or exceeds minimum benefits.

rows.fact_text: Abu Dhabi Law No. 23 of 2005 mandates compulsory health insurance subscription for all non-UAE nationals residing in Abu Dhabi. Employers must provide health coverage through approved insurers including DAMAN (the National Health Insurance Company). The minimum annual benefit limit is AED 150,000. DAMAN administers the Thiqa programme for UAE nationals and Daman Basic for some expat workers.
rows.evidence_quote: Subscription to the health insurance scheme is compulsory for non-UAE nationals and their families who are residing in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi.

rows.fact_text: The minimum required annual health insurance benefit limit in both Dubai and Abu Dhabi is AED 150,000 per person per year. Health insurance must be in place before the employment visa/residence permit is issued. As of 2024, UAE federal regulations are extending mandatory employer-paid health insurance nationwide across all emirates.
rows.evidence_quote: The minimum coverage required is AED 150,000 in annual benefits. All three require a minimum AED 150,000 annual benefit limit.

rows.fact_text: The UAE imposes zero personal income tax on individuals, including expatriate employees. There is no salary tax, employment tax, or payroll tax deducted from employees' wages. Expatriate workers take home 100% of their gross salary net of any voluntary pension or savings scheme contributions.
rows.evidence_quote: CT rates are: 0 per cent for taxable income up to AED 375,000, 9 per cent for taxable income above AED 375,000.

rows.fact_text: UAE Federal Corporate Income Tax of 9% on taxable profits exceeding AED 375,000 (~USD 102,000) per financial year applies from June 2023 onwards under Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022. Profits up to AED 375,000 are taxed at 0%. Small businesses meeting revenue thresholds under the Small Business Relief provision may also be taxed at 0%.
rows.evidence_quote: CT rates are: 0 per cent for taxable income up to AED 375,000, 9 per cent for taxable income above AED 375,000.

rows.fact_text: UAE introduced Value Added Tax (VAT) at 5% from January 1, 2018. VAT applies to most goods and services, including government service fees. Certain categories are zero-rated or exempt (e.g., many healthcare and education services). Businesses with annual taxable supplies exceeding AED 375,000 must register for VAT with the Federal Tax Authority (FTA).
rows.evidence_quote: The UAE introduced a 9% federal corporate tax in June 2023, applied to business profits exceeding AED 375,000 (~$102,000) per financial year.

rows.fact_text: Despite no UAE personal income tax, expatriates may remain liable for taxes in their home country based on citizenship or residency rules. US citizens and permanent residents, for example, must file US federal tax returns regardless of where they live and may owe US taxes on UAE-sourced income (though Foreign Tax Credits and the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion can reduce liability). UK residents who move to UAE may have UK tax obligations depending on their UK domicile status.
rows.evidence_quote: UAE does not levy personal income tax on individuals. As of June 2023, all companies operating in the United Arab Emirates are subject to a new 9% corporate tax.

rows.fact_text: UAE End of Service Gratuity (EOSB) is calculated on basic salary only (excluding allowances, commissions, or bonuses). Formula: 21 days' basic salary per year of service for the first 5 years, then 30 days' basic salary per year for each additional year beyond 5. Total gratuity is capped at a maximum of 2 years' total basic salary.
rows.evidence_quote: For the first five years of service, the employee receives 21 days' wage per year. For each year beyond five, the rate increases to 30 days' wage per year.

rows.fact_text: All private sector employees in the UAE (regardless of nationality) who complete a minimum of 1 year of continuous service are entitled to EOSB. Eligibility applies upon resignation, termination, end of fixed-term contract, mutual agreement, or redundancy. Employees who resign before completing 1 year are not entitled to gratuity. Domestic workers are covered under separate legislation.
rows.evidence_quote: The UAE labor law states that employees are entitled to a gratuity payment upon completion of one year of continuous service.

rows.fact_text: The UAE Wage Protection System (WPS) is a mandatory electronic salary transfer system requiring all private sector employers to pay wages through MOHRE-approved banks, exchange houses, or financial institutions. As of June 2026, employers must pay salaries by the 1st of each month for the prior month. MOHRE monitors compliance in real time; late or missing payments trigger automatic penalties and can result in work permit suspension.
rows.evidence_quote: Employers must transfer at least 85 per cent of the total wages due to their employees on time (where lawful deductions apply).

rows.fact_text: Under Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021 (effective February 2022), the UAE reformed labour ban rules. A one-year labour ban on issuance of a new work permit may still be imposed by MOHRE on employees who resign without serving the contractually required notice period (30, 60, or 90 days) or who commit specified violations. However, automatic bans for all resignations were removed — a ban is no longer automatic for employees who resign with proper notice.
rows.evidence_quote: A labour ban is lifted automatically after the lapse of the ban period imposed by MoHRE.

rows.fact_text: UAE employment contracts must specify a notice period of 30, 60, or 90 days (as agreed). Employees who resign without serving any notice — or who abandon employment — risk a 1-year labour ban. During probation (maximum 6 months), employees leaving the UAE must give 14 days' notice; employees switching UAE jobs must give 30 days' notice.
rows.evidence_quote: Your UAE employment contract may specify an extended notice period between 30-90 days, but any clause requiring more than 90 days cannot be enforced.

rows.fact_text: All tenancy contracts in Dubai must be registered in the Ejari system managed by the Dubai Land Department (DLD) / Real Estate Regulatory Agency (RERA). Registration is mandatory to: connect utilities (DEWA — Dubai Electricity & Water Authority); apply for or renew a residence visa; register children in schools; and for legal enforceability of the lease.
rows.evidence_quote: Ejari is the official registration of your tenancy contract with the Dubai Land Department (DLD). It's the document that makes your lease legal.

rows.fact_text: Ejari registration process: (1) Gather documents: original signed tenancy contract, security deposit receipt, tenant's Emirates ID and passport copy, landlord's passport and title deed. (2) Register via the Dubai REST app (select RERA > Register Ejari Contract), RERA Ejari website, or visit an authorised Ejari Trustee Centre. (3) Pay registration fee of approximately AED 215 + 5% VAT. (4) Receive Ejari certificate. New contracts and renewals both require registration.
rows.evidence_quote: You will need the following documents to complete your Ejari registration: 1. Original signed tenancy contract. 2. Tenant's Emirates ID and copies of their...

rows.fact_text: Ejari registration fee for new and renewed tenancy contracts: approximately AED 215 plus 5% VAT. The renewal Ejari fee is also AED 215 + VAT. Ejari must be renewed annually when the tenancy contract is renewed.
rows.evidence_quote: The renewal fee is AED 215 + VAT. Ejari is an online registration.

rows.fact_text: UAE residence visa overstay fine: AED 50 per day after the 30-day grace period following visa expiry (standard employment visa). Overstay fines can accumulate significantly; maximum penalty can exceed AED 50,000 plus potential deportation and entry ban. Employees whose visa is being cancelled receive a 30-day exit pass to depart or regularise status.
rows.evidence_quote: The Dubai overstay fine — like every emirate's — is a flat AED 50 (about $13.6) per day. Holders enjoy a 30-day grace period after expiration to renew or depart without penalties.

rows.fact_text: UAE employment visa renewal must be initiated at least 30 days before expiry. Steps: medical test (may be waived for some categories); Emirates ID renewal; pay renewal fees; new visa stamp issued. Employees on standard 3-year visas have a 30-day grace period after expiry before overstay fines accrue. Green and Golden Visa holders have a longer grace period of 90–180 days.
rows.evidence_quote: Standard Renewal Process: Initiate 30 days before expiry. Medical test (may be waived for some). Update Emirates ID. Pay renewal fees. New visa stamped.

rows.fact_text: UAE Labour Law explicitly prohibits employers from: charging employees for visa costs; retaining employee passports; withholding wages; employing workers without valid work permits; and transferring sponsorship without employee consent. Violations are investigated by MOHRE and can result in work permit suspension, fines, or criminal charges.
rows.evidence_quote: Employers must NOT: Charge employees for visa costs. Retain employee passports. Withhold wages. Employ workers without valid permits. Transfer sponsorship without consent.

rows.fact_text: UAE Blue Visa (launched 2025): 10-year renewable residency for individuals making extraordinary contributions to environmental conservation, climate science, sustainability, or environmental advocacy. Applicants must demonstrate achievements through published research, award recognition, sustainability project leadership, or climate advocacy work. Open to both UAE residents and international applicants. No property investment required. Initial 180-day multiple-entry exploration visa issued, transitioning to 10-year residency.
rows.evidence_quote: Individuals who have made 'extraordinary contributions' to protect the environment will qualify for the 10-year residency visa.

rows.fact_text: The E-7 visa covers designated special occupations including IT, engineering, finance, architecture, research, corporate management, hospitality, and more. The E-7-1 (Professional) sub-type alone covers 67 roles. Applicants must have relevant qualifications and a confirmed job offer from a Korean employer. The employer must demonstrate that the foreign national's skills cannot easily be filled by the domestic labor market.
rows.evidence_quote: The key concept behind the E-7 visa is that foreign professionals must provide skills that benefit the Korean economy and cannot easily be filled by the domestic labor market.

rows.fact_text: The E-7 visa is divided into four primary sub-types: E-7-1 (Professionals: IT developers, engineers, managers, marketers — 67 roles); E-7-2 (Semi-Professionals: hotel reception, medical coordinators — 10 roles); E-7-3 (General Skilled: shipyard welders, aquaculture technicians — 8 roles); E-7-4 (Skilled Manual: E-9/H-2 visa holders transitioning via the K-Point system). Three special tracks also exist: E-7-S (high-income/advanced tech experts), E-7-T (top elite tech fields), and E-7-Y (young foreigners who grew up in Korea).
rows.evidence_quote: E-7 visas are divided into four main categories based on technical level and occupation. Each has distinct requirements and salary thresholds.

rows.fact_text: Minimum annual salary thresholds for E-7 visas effective from February 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026 (pre-tax): E-7-1: KRW 31.12 million; E-7-2: KRW 25.89 million; E-7-3: KRW 25.89 million; E-7-4: KRW 26.00 million. The salary must be explicitly stated in the employment contract. Only base salary and fixed allowances count — expense reimbursements (meals, travel) are excluded. Large corporations may use the GNI-based standard of approximately KRW 39 million (80% of previous year GNI per capita).
rows.evidence_quote: The Ministry of Justice has released new salary standards effective from February 1, 2026, to December 31, 2026. All figures are pre-tax annual salaries. E-7-1: 31.12 million KRW, E-7-2: 25.89 million KRW, E-7-3: 25.89 million KRW, E-7-4: 26.00 million KRW.

rows.fact_text: E-7-1 visa qualification paths: (1) Master's degree in a relevant field (no experience required); (2) Bachelor's degree plus 1 year of experience in the relevant field; (3) 5+ years of industry-specific work experience without a degree. Preference/exemptions apply for: graduates of Korean universities (experience waived), graduates of top 500 global universities (QS/THE/ARWU, reduced experience requirement), those with 1+ year experience at a Fortune Global 500 company (possible qualification exemption), and those earning at least 1.5x Korean GNI (priority processing).
rows.evidence_quote: Master's degree Relevant to the occupation (no experience required); Bachelor's + 1 year exp. Both degree and experience must be in the field; 5+ years experience Eligible with industry-specific work experience without a degree.

rows.fact_text: E-7 visa application requires documents from both employer and applicant. Employer documents: invitation letter and hiring plan, business registration certificate, proof of meeting employment requirements (local-to-foreign hiring ratio, no tax arrears), employment contract meeting minimum salary standards. Applicant documents: valid passport (6+ months validity), visa application form and photo, degree certificates and transcripts, proof of experience issued by previous employers, criminal background check (notarized/apostilled), and medical checkup certificate. All overseas documents must be translated into Korean or English and apostilled or consular-notarized.
rows.evidence_quote: All overseas documents must be: Translated into Korean or English; Apostilled or consular-notarized.

rows.fact_text: E-7 visa application process: (1) Applicant secures a job offer from a Korean employer — self-sponsorship is not permitted; (2) Employer prepares supporting documentation; (3) Applicant prepares personal documents; (4) If applying from abroad, submit to the local Korean Embassy/Consulate — processing typically takes 2–4 weeks; (5) After approval and entry, apply for an Alien Registration Card (ARC) within 90 days; (6) Register residence at the local immigration office.
rows.evidence_quote: An E-7 visa requires a sponsoring employer in Korea. Foreign nationals cannot self-sponsor an E-7 visa.

rows.fact_text: E-7 visa holders may transition to F-2-7 (Points-Based Residency) after at least 3 consecutive years of professional residency status, provided they accumulate 80+ points on the scoring system. After 5 years of lawful continuous residence on work visa categories (D-7 through E-7) or F-2, holders may apply for F-5 permanent residency (F-5-1 general route). For E-7 holders with a bachelor's degree or higher in a field designated by the Minister of Justice, a fast-track F-5 is available after 3 years of residence.
rows.evidence_quote: The F-2 visa is available through a points-based system based on, among other things, income level, education, experience, Korean language ability, and length of residence in Korea. After maintaining long-term legal residence, some foreign professionals may be granted permanent residency in South Korea under the F-5 category.

rows.fact_text: The D-7 Intra-Company Transfer visa requires the transferee to be an essential professional (executive, senior manager, or specialist) with at least 1 year of work experience at the foreign headquarters, public institution, or organization. Simple administrative staff or skilled laborers do not qualify. Exception: where more than USD 500,000 in operating funds has been introduced to the Korean branch, applicants with less than 1 year of experience may be considered.
rows.evidence_quote: Mandatory Requirement: You must be an essential professional with at least one year of work experience at must be included. Definition of Essential Professional: This refers to Executives, Senior Managers, and Specialists.

rows.fact_text: The D-7 visa maximum total duration is 5 years. Under the Immigration Control Act, holders who have resided for more than 5 years on D-7 status may be eligible to change to F-5 permanent residency (F-5-1 general category) if other conditions are met, including stable income and tax compliance. Extensions are subject to proof of continued business activity at the Korean branch.
rows.evidence_quote: Those who have resided in Korea for over 5 years with D-7(Intra-Company Transferee)~E-7(Foreign National of Special Ability) visa or F-2(Resident) visa are eligible for permanent residency.

rows.fact_text: Before applying for a D-7 visa, the employer must establish a legitimate Korean branch or liaison office. Required documents include: the installation report (for a branch: 'Report of Installation of a Domestic Branch of a Foreign Corporation'; for a liaison office: 'Unique Business Number' issuance), business registration certificate, lease agreement, Foreign Exchange Purchase Certificate proving operating funds remitted from headquarters, labor contract, and proof of the applicant's headquarters work experience. Visa extensions require tax payment certificates and evidence of ongoing headquarters-branch business exchange.
rows.evidence_quote: Key Documents: The installation report, business registration, lease agreement, and Foreign Exchange Purchase Certificate (proving operating funds sent from the headquarters) must be included.

rows.fact_text: The D-7 visa does not have a fixed statutory minimum salary equivalent to the E-7 requirements, but immigration requires proof of compensation commensurate with professional standards and the scale of the Korean branch. A monthly salary of at least KRW 3.4 million is generally recommended. The salary may be paid by the headquarters or the Korean branch, but must be documented via employment contract or dispatch order proving the income covers Korean living costs. The 2026 GNI is KRW 52.41 million, which is used as a benchmark for accompanying family sponsorship.
rows.evidence_quote: Screening Criteria: You must prove that you receive compensation suitable for the position and the scale of the branch (usually recommended to be at least 3.4 million KRW per month).

rows.fact_text: Spouses and minor children of D-7 visa holders enter Korea on an F-3 (accompanying family) visa. As of 2026, the spouse of a D-7 holder may be employed in professional fields after obtaining an 'Employment Permit for Status Outside of Stay' from the immigration office. Simple labor or service jobs remain prohibited for F-3 visa holders. Children have free access to public schools and international schools equivalent to Korean nationals.
rows.evidence_quote: Employment Permit: As of 2026, the spouse of an expatriate may be employed in professional fields after receiving an 'Employment Permit for Status Outside of Stay' from the immigration office. However, simple labor or service jobs (like restaurant waiting) remain prohibited.

rows.fact_text: The D-8 Corporate Investment visa (D-8-1) requires a minimum investment of KRW 100 million (approximately USD 75,000) in a Korean corporation under the Foreign Investment Promotion Act. The investor must acquire at least 10% of the total voting shares of the Korean company. The capital must originate from outside South Korea and be confirmed via a Foreign Currency Purchase Certificate or bank-issued overseas remittance confirmation. Passive 'paper' investments are frequently rejected under heightened 2026 consular scrutiny.
rows.evidence_quote: Minimum Investment: KRW 100 million (approx. USD 75,000). Equity Threshold: You must acquire at least 10% of the voting shares of the Korean company. Fund Origin: Funds must be transferred from overseas.

rows.fact_text: The D-8-4 (Technology Startup) visa is a points-based route for foreign founders launching a new Korean corporation. Eligibility requires: a Bachelor's degree (from any country) or an Associate's degree from a Korean university; establishment of a brand-new corporation (acquiring an existing entity is not eligible); and a score of at least 80 points out of 368 total via the OASIS (Overall Assistance for Startup Immigration System) program. At least one mandatory OASIS item must be completed (e.g., holding intellectual property rights or completing specific training modules).
rows.evidence_quote: Point System: You must score at least 80 points out of a total 368. Mandatory items: You must satisfy at least one mandatory item (e.g., holding intellectual property rights like a patent, or completing specific OASIS training modules).

rows.fact_text: D-8-4 (Technology Startup) visa holders may access an F-5 permanent residency fast-track after 3 years of residence if they attract KRW 300 million or more in investment from external sources and employ at least two Korean citizens for at least 6 months. For D-8-1 (Corporate Investment) holders, F-5 eligibility generally requires at least 5 years of lawful residence. Investors with USD 500,000 or more may have Korean language proficiency and minimum stay requirements waived or significantly reduced.
rows.evidence_quote: After 3 years of residence if you: Attract KRW 300 million or more in investment. Employ at least two Korean citizens for at least 6 months.

rows.fact_text: The E-2 (Foreign Language Instructor) visa for English teaching is restricted to citizens of 7 designated countries: United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and Ireland. Indian nationals may qualify under the Korea-India CEPA agreement with a bachelor's degree and a certified English teaching qualification. Applicants must hold a Bachelor's degree or higher in any field from a university in their home country. The language taught must be the applicant's native language.
rows.evidence_quote: For English teaching specifically, only citizens of these 7 countries are eligible for the standard E-2 route: United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Ireland.

rows.fact_text: All E-2 visa applicants must submit a national-level criminal background check (not a local check) from their country of citizenship, authenticated with an apostille. For US citizens this is the FBI background check. The check must be apostilled and is valid for 6 months from the date of issue — it should be the last document obtained due to this time limit. The apostille process typically takes 8–12 weeks for US applicants. Zero tolerance for criminal convictions applies.
rows.evidence_quote: A national-level background check with a clean record. Zero tolerance for criminal convictions. The check must be apostilled and is valid for 6 months from the date of issue.

rows.fact_text: E-2 visa applicants must provide the original degree certificate (bachelor's or higher) plus a copy. The degree must be apostilled if from a Hague Convention country. Consular verification is required for degrees from non-Hague countries. A certified Korean or English translation of the degree is required. Additionally, a medical examination (including drug test) must be passed upon arrival in Korea, and a sealed medical test result (TB and HIV) is required for the ARC application.
rows.evidence_quote: Bachelor's degree (or higher) Original + copy. Must be apostilled if from a Hague Convention country. Consular verification required if not. Certified Korean or English translation required.

rows.fact_text: E-2 visa holders may teach at public schools (via EPIK — English Program in Korea, administered by the Ministry of Education), private language academies (hagwon), universities, corporate training programs, and the TaLK government scholarship program. Monthly salary ranges (2026): EPIK KRW 1.8–2.65 million; hagwon KRW 2.0–2.8 million; university KRW 2.2–3.5 million+; corporate KRW 2.5–4.0 million. All E-2 employers must by law provide: National Health Insurance, National Pension, severance pay (1 month per year), and paid annual leave from 1 year of service.
rows.evidence_quote: Mandatory benefits under Korean law: (1) National Health Insurance — employer pays 50%, (2) National Pension — employer pays 50%, (3) Severance pay — 1 month's salary per year worked, paid at contract end, (4) Paid annual leave starting from 1 year of service.

rows.fact_text: The F-2-7 (Points-Based Highly Skilled Talent) visa requires a minimum total score of 80 points on the official scoring table. Applicants fall into 5 target categories: (1) Employees of publicly listed companies (KOSPI/KOSDAQ); (2) Employees in promising industrial fields (IT, nano, bio, etc.) with prior year income ≥1.5× GNI; (3) Professional workers who have resided lawfully for 3+ consecutive years on E-1 through E-7-1, D-5 through D-9 status; (4) Study achievers who completed a master's degree or higher in Korea and secured qualifying employment within 5 years; (5) Potential high-skilled talents (F-2-7S) — master's/doctoral from science/engineering institutions (no points or employment required).
rows.evidence_quote: F-2-7 high-skilled talent scorecard: application is possible if the total score is 80 points or above. The applicants are divided into a total of 5 categories.

rows.fact_text: For the F-2-7 professional worker category, the applicant must have resided legally and continuously in Korea for more than 3 years under professional status (E-1 to E-7-1, D-5 to D-9). The 3-year residency requirement is waived if: (a) the annual income on the Certificate of Income Amount exceeds KRW 40 million, or (b) the applicant is recognized by the Minister of Justice as a participant in a foreign talent attraction project with a recommendation from a central government agency.
rows.evidence_quote: Must have legally stayed continuously for more than 3 years under the professional residency status listed above at the time of application. The residency period requirement (3 years) is waived if annual income exceeds 40 million won.

rows.fact_text: The spouse and minor children of an F-2-7 holder may receive F-2-71 status (which allows free employment in most sectors) if the principal holder's prior year income meets or exceeds 1× the GNI (KRW 42.2 million in 2023; indexed annually). If the income threshold is not met, family members receive F-1-12 status, which restricts employment activities. The F-2-71 spouse may not work in restricted sectors (entertainment bars, gambling establishments, youth-harmful businesses).
rows.evidence_quote: Annual income requirement (at least 1 times the GNI in 2023 = more than 42.2 million won). Accompanying family can apply for F-2-71 simultaneously when the principal holder applies for F-2-7.

rows.fact_text: The F-4 (Overseas Korean) visa is available to individuals of Korean descent who hold foreign citizenship — specifically those whose parents or grandparents previously held Korean nationality, or who themselves formerly held Korean citizenship before acquiring foreign nationality. As of the most recent policy expansion, all ethnic Koreans from abroad regardless of country of origin are eligible for F-4, effectively ending the H-2 visa for this group. The visa is typically issued for 3-year periods with multiple entry, and holders can freely change employers without a separate immigration permit.
rows.evidence_quote: The F-4 visa is still worth pursuing based on its advantages: the longer period of stay for which it is typically issued (the F-4 visa is usually issued for three years); the freedom to change employers without a separate immigration permit; and the absence of associated quota issues.

rows.fact_text: Since 2019, F-4 visa applicants must obtain an apostilled police clearance certificate from their country of nationality AND from each country in which they have resided for at least 1 year during the 5-year period preceding the application. Obtaining the police clearance certificate plus apostille can take up to 10 weeks in some countries. Applicants who did not previously hold Korean nationality must also submit Korean language test results. The overall lead time for an F-4 application is significantly longer than before 2019.
rows.evidence_quote: F-4 visa applicants must now obtain an apostilled police clearance certificate from their country of nationality and from each country in which they have resided for at least one year (during the five-year period preceding the F-4 visa application).

rows.fact_text: F-4 visa holders may apply for F-5 permanent residency (overseas Korean permanent residency category) after residing in Korea for at least 2 years with F-4 status, provided they meet other requirements including stable income, tax compliance, and no immigration violations. This is one of the faster permanent residency routes for ethnic Koreans with foreign citizenship.
rows.evidence_quote: You can apply for permanent residence for overseas Koreans if you have been living in Korea for at least two years with an F4 visa.

rows.fact_text: F-5 permanent residency has 26 eligibility categories. The primary general route (F-5-1) requires 5+ years of lawful continuous residence on professional/business visa categories (D-7 through E-7) or F-2 residency status. Applicants must demonstrate: stable income, regular tax payments, no immigration law violations, and Korean integration (language ability, assets). The F-5-16 fast-track allows F-2-7 holders to apply for F-5 after 3 years from F-2-7 initial issuance date.
rows.evidence_quote: F-5-1 General Permanent Resident: 5+ years lawful stay on D-7~E-7 or F-2 residency status.

rows.fact_text: All foreigners staying in South Korea for a period exceeding 90 days must apply for an Alien Registration Card (now officially called the Residence Card / RC) within 90 days of arrival. The card was officially renamed from Alien Registration Card to Residence Card in 2024, though 'ARC' remains in common use. Missing the 90-day deadline can result in administrative fines and may complicate future visa renewals and extensions. Walk-in visits to immigration offices are generally not accepted — appointments must be reserved through HiKorea (www.hikorea.go.kr) in advance.
rows.evidence_quote: You must apply for a residence card within 90 days of arriving in Korea. Missing the 90-day deadline can result in administrative fines and may complicate future visa renewals and extensions.

rows.fact_text: Documents required for the ARC / Residence Card application: (1) Residence Card application form; (2) Original passport + photocopy; (3) Passport-sized photo (3.5 × 4.5 cm, white background, taken within 6 months); (4) Sealed medical test results (TB and HIV; envelope must remain unopened); (5) Photocopy of accommodation contract (lease or housing agreement); (6) Signed confirmation letter of accommodation residency (landlord or school signature); (7) KRW 35,000 application fee (cash only as of 2025); (8) Employer-provided documentation such as a copy of school registration license (for E-2 teachers). Medical exam fee ranges KRW 60,000–150,000.
rows.evidence_quote: ₩35,000 Application fee (as of 2025). Up to 6 Weeks Processing time. 8 Items Required documents.

rows.fact_text: The ARC / Residence Card processing takes up to 6 weeks after submission. The card functions as both a social security number (unique identification number) and a national ID card for foreigners. It is essential for accessing: mobile phone plans and SIM registration, Korean bank account opening, internet service contracts, National Health Insurance enrollment, National Pension enrollment, and credit card applications. Applicants may opt for mail delivery of the card for a small additional fee or collect it in person at the immigration office. A digital mobile ARC has been available since January 2025 (not mandatory for holders with cards issued before that date).
rows.evidence_quote: An ARC (Alien Registration Card) is now referred to as the Residence Card (RC). A residence card is essential for signing up for services like mobile phone plans, internet, banking, and even health insurance and pension enrollment.

rows.fact_text: National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) enrollment is mandatory for foreign residents on long-stay visas (D, E, F series) who reside in Korea for 6 months or more, a rule introduced in July 2019. Employed workers are enrolled from Day 1 of employment through their employer as 'workplace subscribers' (직장가입자) — the 6-month waiting period does not apply to employed foreigners. Self-employed or unemployed foreigners become 'regional subscribers' (지역가입자) after 6 months and pay premiums directly. NHIS multilingual hotline: 1577-1000 ext. 6 (English available).
rows.evidence_quote: NHIS enrollment is mandatory for foreign residents in Korea after six months. Employed workers are enrolled from day one through their employer as workplace subscribers.

rows.fact_text: The 2026 NHIS contribution rate for employed workers is 7.19% of salary (effective January 1, 2026), split evenly between employer and employee: 3.595% deducted from the employee's pay and 3.595% paid by the employer. NHIS revises the rate annually. The rate is applied to gross salary. D-2 international students receive a 50% premium reduction (as of March 2023). NHIS covers 60–80% of most medical costs including doctor visits, hospital stays, prescriptions, and surgeries. Major exclusions: most dental care, vision correction, cosmetic procedures, and elective MRIs.
rows.evidence_quote: Monthly premiums for employed foreigners are 7.19% of salary at the 2026 rate (effective Jan 1, 2026), split evenly: 3.595% deducted from your pay, 3.595% paid by your employer.

rows.fact_text: NHIS covers: 60–80% of doctor visits, clinics, and hospital stays; 60–80% of most prescription medications; most surgeries and inpatient care; basic lab tests and imaging (CT, X-ray); medically necessary MRI ordered by a doctor. Patient copay rates vary by facility type: approximately 30% at a local clinic (의원), 40% at a hospital (병원), 50% at a general hospital (종합병원), and higher at tertiary hospitals without a referral. Tertiary hospitals (e.g., Samsung Medical Center, Severance, Asan) require a referral letter for NHIS coverage on specialist outpatient consultations.
rows.evidence_quote: Outpatient copay rates scale by facility type: roughly 30% at a local clinic, 40% at a hospital, and 50% at a general hospital.

rows.fact_text: Foreigners working in South Korea are required to contribute to the National Pension Service (NPS) scheme unless specifically exempt. Both the employer and employee each contribute 4.5% of monthly wages, for a total contribution rate of 9%. NPS contributions are mandatory for most work visa holders (E-7, D-7, D-8, E-2, etc.). Foreigners from countries with totalization agreements are eligible to claim exemption from Korean NPS contributions if they remain covered by their home country's pension system.
rows.evidence_quote: Foreigners working in Korea are required to contribute to the NP scheme. Both employers and employees contribute 4.5% of monthly wages, creating a total contribution rate of 9%.

rows.fact_text: Korea has concluded Social Security (Totalization) Agreements with 38+ countries including: United States (in force April 2001), United Kingdom, Germany, Canada, China, Japan, Australia, France, Italy, Netherlands, Belgium, Poland, India, Brazil, and others. Under these agreements, workers transferred from their home country to Korea for less than 5 years (extendable to up to 9 years with agency consent) may remain covered by the home country pension system and be exempt from Korean NPS contributions. Employers must obtain a Certificate of Coverage from the home country authority to establish the exemption.
rows.evidence_quote: A detached worker is exempt from coverage under the laws of the contracting country which he/she is sent to for less than 5 years if he/she is covered under the laws of his/her home country. This 5-year limit can be extended to 9 years with the proper consent between Agencies of both countries.

rows.fact_text: Foreign nationals who have paid into the Korean NPS and depart Korea permanently are entitled to a lump-sum refund (반환일시금) of their accumulated pension contributions plus interest. To claim, applicants must have made at least 1 month of contributions and have departed Korea. The refund can be claimed from overseas by submitting an application to the NPS or to the competent institution in the home country (for totalization agreement countries). The lump-sum refund is not available to nationals of countries whose home pension system does not provide equivalent reciprocal treatment to Korean nationals.
rows.evidence_quote: Benefits under this Agreement. Even though your periods of coverage in one country are not sufficient to qualify for pension benefits, you may be eligible for benefits after this Agreement has entered into force. This is possible due to totalization of coverage in both countries.

rows.fact_text: Employment Insurance (EI) is generally mandatory for employees in South Korea, including most foreign workers. The 2026 EI contribution rate is 1.8% of monthly salary, split between employer and employee (each contributing 0.9%). Employers make additional contributions of 0.25%–0.85% for employment stability and job skills development programs beyond the basic 0.9%. Foreigners from countries without reciprocal EI arrangements may be exempt from EI obligations — exemption is determined by nationality and visa type.
rows.evidence_quote: Employment Insurance (EI) 0.9% (employee) 1.15% to 1.75% (employer). EI contribution rates remain at 1.8% of monthly salary in 2026 (employer and employee each contribute 0.9%).

rows.fact_text: Foreign residents holding an ARC/Residence Card must register their Korean address (체류지, cheryuji) with the local immigration office and, separately, may register at the dong (동) or gu (구) office — equivalent to the jumindeungnok (resident registration) for Korean citizens. The registered address appears on the ARC/Residence Card. When moving, foreign residents must report a change of address to the immigration office within 14 days. Failure to report a change of address may result in fines. Address registration is required to receive official mail and to access certain government services.
rows.evidence_quote: The newer format has your registered address in Korea (체류지, 滯留地, cheryuji) and the date it was modified.

rows.fact_text: Foreign workers in South Korea can open a bank account at all major commercial banks once they have their ARC / Residence Card. Required documents typically include: ARC/Residence Card (essential), valid passport with visa, a Korean phone number capable of receiving SMS/OTP, and proof of address. KEB Hana Bank and Woori Bank are among the banks popular with expatriates. Some banks require a Certificate of Employment. The ARC number serves as the primary account registration identifier. Foreigners with ARC can also apply for credit cards and internet banking.
rows.evidence_quote: You will typically need: your passport (with visa), your ARC or mobile ARC, a Korean phone number capable of receiving SMS and OTP messages, proof of address.

rows.fact_text: Opening a Korean bank account requires a local Korean phone number (mobile) for SMS and OTP (one-time password) authentication. This creates a dependency loop: SIM registration requires the ARC, and bank account opening requires a phone number. The recommended sequence is: (1) obtain ARC; (2) purchase a local SIM using ARC; (3) open a bank account using ARC plus phone number. Some banks (including KEB Hana) have English-language services and expat-focused branches in major cities.
rows.evidence_quote: What You Need to Open a Korean Bank Account: Passport, Valid visa, Alien Registration Card (ARC), Your Korean address (in English and Korean), Korean phone number.

rows.fact_text: Sponsoring employers for E-7 visas must demonstrate: legitimate and sustainable business operations in Korea; that hiring a foreign professional is justified and essential for operations; a business registration certificate; tax records and financial statements; a business plan; an employment contract; a detailed job description; and an explanation of why a foreign national is needed. The company must also meet the local-to-foreign hiring ratio requirement and have no tax arrears. Companies face annual quotas on the number of foreign E-7 employees relative to Korean staff, with stricter caps for smaller companies.
rows.evidence_quote: The sponsoring company must demonstrate that the company has legitimate and sustainable business operations in Korea. Hiring a foreign professional is justified, necessary, and essential for the company's operations.

rows.fact_text: Common reasons for E-7 visa rejection include: (1) Incorrect job classification — when actual job duties do not precisely match the designated E-7 occupation code; (2) Insufficient salary — not meeting the applicable minimum threshold; (3) Unrelated academic or experience background — degrees/experience outside the relevant field; (4) Employer compliance issues — sponsoring company cannot demonstrate legitimate operations; (5) Discrepancies across documents — job title, location, duties, and pay varying across submitted forms.
rows.evidence_quote: Common Legal Issues: 1. Incorrect Job Classification; 2. Insufficient Salary; 3. Unrelated Academic or Experience Background; 4. Employer Compliance Issues.

rows.fact_text: E-7 visas are generally issued as multiple-entry visas, allowing the holder to leave and re-enter South Korea during the visa validity period without applying for a new visa. The initial visa is typically issued for 1 year from the date of issuance, with extensions available in 1–2 year increments up to a maximum per-stay period. E-7 holders who maintain their employment relationship may continue renewing their visa status.
rows.evidence_quote: Multiple Entry Standard: most work visas are multiple entry by default.

rows.fact_text: South Korea introduced a digital mobile ARC (mobile Residence Card) in January 2025. The mobile ARC functions as a digital version of the physical card and can be used for most identification purposes. It is not mandatory for holders whose physical cards were issued before January 1, 2025. Existing physical ARC holders do not need to apply for the digital version, but new applicants may opt for the mobile ARC. The physical card remains the primary accepted document at immigration checkpoints.
rows.evidence_quote: It is not mandatory for ARC holders with cards issued before January 1, 2025, to apply for the digital ARC. The mobile ARC will be available from January 2025.

rows.fact_text: For the E-7-4 pathway (K-Point system), the maximum score is 300 points across categories: Average Income (max 120 points — highest scores for income ≥ KRW 33 million per year); Korean Proficiency (max 120 points — TOPIK Level 2 required minimum; Level 5+ gives maximum points); Age (max 60 points — ages 18–39 are favored); Bonus Points (max 70 points — for domestic assets ≥ KRW 100 million, relevant degrees, etc.); Deductions (-50 points for immigration law violations or criminal records). A score of 200+ out of 300 is required for E-7-4 qualification. TOPIK Level 4 or higher significantly increases success chances.
rows.evidence_quote: Basic Requirements 4+ years of legal employment within the last 10 years. Currently employed with a 2-year employment contract. Score 200+ out of 300 total points.

rows.fact_text: The D-8-1 (Corporate Investment) visa application follows a strict sequence: (1) File a Foreign Investment Report with a designated Korean bank or KOTRA before remitting any money; (2) Remit KRW 100 million+ to a temporary capital subscription account at the Korean bank; (3) Complete share purchase or capital increase so the Korean company issues new shares; (4) Update the corporate registry at the local court to reflect new ownership/directorship; (5) Obtain the Foreign-Invested Enterprise (FIE) Registration Certificate from the bank; (6) Submit the full visa application to the Korean Embassy (if abroad) or Immigration Office (if already in Korea on a valid long-term visa).
rows.evidence_quote: Foreign Investment Report: Notify a Korean bank or KOTRA before sending any money. Remit Capital: Send the KRW 100M+ to a temporary 'capital subscription account' at the Korean bank.

rows.fact_text: Under the US-Korea Social Security Totalization Agreement (in force April 2001), workers who have paid into both systems may combine (totalize) their periods of coverage to qualify for benefits. Korean NPS requires at least 20 years of coverage for a full old-age pension; reduced pension is available with at least 10 years of coverage from age 60 (age 65 for those born 1968 or later). If a worker has at least 18 months of NPS contributions but insufficient total years to qualify, they may totalize US Social Security credits to meet the threshold. Similar provisions exist for agreement countries including UK, Germany, Canada, Australia, Japan, and others.
rows.evidence_quote: If you have more than 18 months of insured period in Korea but do not have enough periods of coverage (e.g., 20 years for Full Old-age pension) to qualify for pension benefits under the Korean pension system, you may be able to qualify for Korean benefits by totalizing periods of coverage under the Korean pension system and the American pension system.

rows.fact_text: E-2 visa holders must complete a full medical examination at a designated hospital in Korea within 90 days of arrival. The exam includes tests for tuberculosis (TB), HIV, and general health including drug screening. The sealed medical test results (envelope must remain unopened) are a required document for the ARC application. Medical exam fees range from KRW 60,000 to KRW 150,000. Appointments are strongly recommended. The ARC application cannot proceed without the sealed medical results.
rows.evidence_quote: The medical exam checks for general health conditions, drug use, and specific diseases. The exam typically includes an X-ray, a blood test, and other physical tests.

rows.fact_text: D-7 visa holders with high educational background and high salary may transition to F-2-7 (Points-Based Residency) after at least 3 years of professional residency in Korea, providing the freedom to change jobs or start a business in Korea. A further F-5-16 (Permanent Residency) fast-track is available after 3 years on F-2-7. D-7 holders who remain on professional work visas for 5+ years are eligible for the F-5-1 general permanent residency route without going through F-2-7.
rows.evidence_quote: F-2-7 (Points-based Residence): Expatriates with high educational background and salary can switch to a points-based residence visa, gaining the freedom to change jobs or start a business in Korea. F-5-16 (Permanent Residency): A fast-track exists to apply for permanent residency after staying for at least 3 years on a residence visa.

rows.fact_text: Dependents of NHIS workplace subscribers (employed foreigners) must have 6 months of Korea residency to qualify as enrolled dependents, except for the subscriber's spouse and children under 19 (rule effective April 2024 — the waiting period is waived for spouses and minor children of employed workers from the date of the worker's enrollment). Self-employed/regional subscriber dependents also require 6 months of Korean residence to be covered.
rows.evidence_quote: Dependents need 6 months of Korea residency to qualify, except workplace subscribers' spouses and children under 19 (rule effective April 2024).

rows.fact_text: A special F-5 permanent residency route exists for high-value investors. For D-8 corporate investors, investment of USD 500,000 or more in a Korean corporation (with job creation) significantly eases F-5 eligibility — Korean language proficiency requirements and minimum stay durations may be waived or substantially reduced. The general D-8-4 startup track requires attracting KRW 300 million in external investment and employing at least 2 Korean nationals for 6 months before being eligible for the F-5 fast-track after 3 years.
rows.evidence_quote: If you plan to eventually apply for Permanent Residency (F-5), consider increasing your investment to USD 500,000. At this level, many requirements like Korean language proficiency and minimum stay duration are waived or significantly eased.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA nationals employed by a Swiss company for up to 3 months per calendar year do not require a residence permit but must use the electronic notification procedure. Also covers posted workers from EU/EFTA companies (including third-country nationals with 12+ months prior EU/EFTA residence) and self-employed service providers from EU/EFTA states.
rows.evidence_quote: Citizens of EU/EFTA member states do not require a residence permit to take up employment with a company in Switzerland for a period of up to three months per calendar year. Nevertheless, such employment requires the electronic notification of short-term stays.

rows.fact_text: For EU/EFTA nationals hired by Swiss employers for short stays, notification must be submitted no later than the day before starting work (one day prior). For posted workers and self-employed service providers, the standard rule is 8 days before commencement. Emergency exceptions (repairs, accidents, natural disasters completed within 3 calendar days) allow same-day notification.
rows.evidence_quote: The employer has to submit an online notification form no later than the day before starting work.

rows.fact_text: Notification is submitted electronically via the easygov.swiss online portal. Paper forms are only permitted if online notification is technically impossible. Companies and service providers must create user profiles in the system before submitting. Staff leasing from abroad to Switzerland is not permitted under any circumstances.
rows.evidence_quote: The online notification procedure is the standard method through easygov.swiss. Paper forms may be submitted only if online notification over the Internet is not possible for technical reasons.

rows.fact_text: The notification procedure covers work up to 90 effective working days per calendar year. Days are counted cumulatively per self-employed person or per company posting staff. High-risk sectors (construction, gardening, hospitality, cleaning, security, itinerant trade, sex work) require notification from the first day regardless of duration.
rows.evidence_quote: Up to 90 effective working days per calendar year without requiring a work permit. The 8-day notification-free period applies per calendar year before notification becomes mandatory.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA nationals with an employment contract between 3 and 12 months are entitled to an L EU/EFTA permit (short-stay permit). The permit's validity period matches the employment contract duration. Extensions are possible for a total period of less than 12 months. Also available to EU/EFTA job seekers (no entitlement to social assistance).
rows.evidence_quote: For employment lasting between three months and one year, workers are entitled to a short-stay permit (L EU/EFTA), whose period of validity matches the duration of the employment contract.

rows.fact_text: To obtain an L EU/EFTA permit, applicants must present: a valid identity card or passport, and a written confirmation of employment (e.g. employment contract specifying duration and number of working hours). The residence permit doubles as work permit when accompanied by written employment confirmation.
rows.evidence_quote: A valid ID or passport and a written confirmation of employment (e.g. the contract of employment containing details of the duration of employment and the number of working hours)

rows.fact_text: L EU/EFTA permits are issued by the cantonal migration office (Migrationsamt/Office cantonal de la population) of the canton where the applicant resides. The applicant must register at the commune of residence within 14 days of arrival and before taking up work, and apply for the permit there.
rows.evidence_quote: The cantons are responsible for issuing permits. For detailed information on the application procedure (where to apply, which form to fill out, how long it will take, etc.), please contact the competent cantonal authorities.

rows.fact_text: For EU/EFTA students on an L permit who want to work: the employer must submit an application, and standard employment conditions must be met. Students may work up to 15 hours per week outside holidays after the first 6 months of study, with university confirmation that work is compatible with studies.
rows.evidence_quote: foreign students may work for a maximum of 15 hours a week outside of the holidays. However, the university authorities must confirm that the student's work is compatible with their studies.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA nationals with an employment contract of at least 12 months or of unlimited duration are issued a B EU/EFTA permit valid for 5 years. No labour-market test applies. The permit is renewable for successive 5-year periods as long as conditions continue to be met. First renewal may be limited to 1 year if involuntary unemployment exceeded 12 consecutive months.
rows.evidence_quote: For employment lasting for one year, several years or for an unlimited duration, workers will be issued a residence permit (B EU/EFTA), which remains valid for a period of five years.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA nationals without gainful employment (economically inactive) are also entitled to a B permit if they can prove they have sufficient financial means and adequate health and accident insurance. No employment contract required. Applies to retirees and financially independent persons.
rows.evidence_quote: Nationals from all EU/EFTA member states without gainful employment are entitled to a B permit if they can prove they have sufficient financial means and adequate health and accident insurance.

rows.fact_text: For EU/EFTA nationals, the B residence permit doubles as a work permit when accompanied by written confirmation of employment. Permit holders are entitled to change jobs and occupations freely anywhere in Switzerland without additional authorisation. Permit is valid for the whole of Switzerland.
rows.evidence_quote: A residence permit doubles as work permit but only if accompanied by written confirmation of employment showing duration and hours.

rows.fact_text: Spouses and children of EU/EFTA B permit holders have the right to work anywhere in Switzerland and in the branch of their choice, without needing additional authorisation procedures. Employment duration is limited to the spouse's permit validity. Applies regardless of the spouse's or child's nationality.
rows.evidence_quote: Spouses and children of holders of permanent residence permits have the right to work, without needing to go through any additional authorisation procedure.

rows.fact_text: Spouses and family members of L permit holders (short-term, 3–12 months) may be given permission to pursue gainful employment if an employer submits an application on their behalf. Salary, social security contributions, terms of employment, and personal qualifications must meet the required standards.
rows.evidence_quote: Members of the family of holders of a short-term residence ('L') permit may be given permission to pursue gainful employment if an application is submitted by an employer and standard employment conditions are met.

rows.fact_text: Settlement permit (C) granted to EU/EFTA nationals from treaty countries after 5 years regular and uninterrupted residence. Treaty countries include: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, and EFTA states (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway). Once granted, right is not subject to time restrictions or conditions.
rows.evidence_quote: foreign nationals who have been granted a settlement permit after five or ten years' residence in Switzerland... after five years' regular and uninterrupted residence in Switzerland.

rows.fact_text: EU member states NOT covered by C permit settlement treaties include: Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Cyprus, Slovenia. Nationals of these countries do not qualify for the C permit under settlement treaties but may qualify under FNIA after 10 years (general rule for third-country-equivalent treatment applies).
rows.evidence_quote: No such treaties exist for nationals of the other EU member states.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA nationals wishing to work in a self-employed capacity in Switzerland will initially receive a B EU/EFTA permit valid for 5 years, if they demonstrate the existence of an effective self-employed activity when submitting their application. No labour-market test or quota applies.
rows.evidence_quote: EU/EFTA citizens wishing to work in a self-employed capacity in Switzerland will initially receive a B EU/EFTA permit valid for five years – if they are able to show the existence of an effective self-employed activity when submitting their application.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA self-employed persons must register within 14 days of arrival at the latest with the local authorities of the commune and apply for a B residence permit. They must present a valid identity card (or passport) and documents proving self-employed activity and ability to self-support and support family members.
rows.evidence_quote: EU/EFTA citizens are required to register within 14 days of arrival at the latest with the local authorities of the commune in which they are residing and apply for a residence permit. They must present a valid identity card (or passport) and documents proving that they are or will be engaged in a self-employed activity.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA students are issued a student residence permit for 1 year, with annual renewals until the completion of studies, provided they continue to meet conditions. Students must demonstrate admission to a state-recognised institution of learning and ability to support themselves financially for the duration of studies.
rows.evidence_quote: Students are issued this permit for one year and are granted yearly renewals until the completion of their studies, if they continue to fulfil the respective conditions. Students must show admission to a state-recognized institution of learning, and that they can support themselves for the duration of their studies.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA student permit holders must apply for extension/renewal 14 days before the current permit expires. Annual renewals are granted if the student continues to meet conditions (enrolled, self-supporting).
rows.evidence_quote: Students must apply for an extension to their permit 14 days before it expires.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA students (and third-country students) in Switzerland may work a maximum of 15 hours per week outside of holidays, beginning no sooner than 6 months after the start of their course at a Swiss university or university of applied sciences. The employer must apply and the university must confirm compatibility with studies.
rows.evidence_quote: Beginning no sooner than six months after the start of their course, foreign students may work for a maximum of 15 hours a week outside of the holidays. However, the university authorities must confirm that the student's work is compatible with their studies.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA students may apply for family reunification for their spouses and dependent children only. They cannot sponsor dependent parents under the student route (unlike employed EU/EFTA nationals). The same accommodation requirement applies.
rows.evidence_quote: Students and persons undergoing training may only apply for family reunification for their spouses and dependent children.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA nationals holding a Swiss residence permit or short-stay permit may bring: (1) their spouse and their own or spouse's children under 21 or who are financially dependent; (2) their own or spouse's parents who are financially dependent — this last option is NOT available to students. Applies regardless of the family members' nationality.
rows.evidence_quote: EU/EFTA nationals holding a Swiss residence permit or short-stay permit for EU/EFTA citizens may bring: their spouse as well as their own children or their spouse's children (who are under the age of 21 or receive support); their own parents or their spouse's parents who receive support (this option is not available for students).

rows.fact_text: Anyone wishing to bring family to Switzerland must have suitable accommodation. Accommodation is deemed suitable if it reflects typical living conditions of Swiss citizens. No specific square-metre requirement is set in the factsheet; it is assessed relative to Swiss standards.
rows.evidence_quote: Anyone wishing to bring his/her family to Switzerland must have suitable accommodation. An accommodation is deemed suitable if it reflects typical living conditions of Swiss citizens.

rows.fact_text: If the EU/EFTA main applicant is an employee, the right to family reunification is NOT contingent upon their financial situation — no income test applies. Self-employed persons and economically inactive persons may only apply for family reunification if they have the necessary financial means to support the family members.
rows.evidence_quote: If the main entitled person is an employee, then the right to family reunification is not contingent upon that person's financial situation. Self-employed persons or economically inactive persons may only apply for family reunification if they have the necessary financial means to support these family members.

rows.fact_text: Family members applying for residence permit under EU family reunification must present: (1) valid identity card or passport; (2) visa if non-EU/EFTA and subject to visa requirement (Schengen residence permit holders exempt); (3) certificate from country of origin confirming family relationship to EU/EFTA citizen in Switzerland; (4) for dependent relatives: certificate from country of origin confirming dependency or cohabitation.
rows.evidence_quote: In order to obtain a residence permit, family members must present: a valid identity card or passport; a visa (for non EU/EFTA citizens who are subject to a visa requirement); a certificate issued by the authorities of the country of origin confirming that the person is a family member of the EU/EFTA citizen living in Switzerland.

rows.fact_text: Family members who come to Switzerland under EU/EFTA family reunification (spouse and children under 21 or dependent) have the right to work anywhere in Switzerland and in any branch of their choice, including self-employment, regardless of their nationality. Ascending-line relatives (parents, grandparents) who enter via family reunification do NOT have the right to work.
rows.evidence_quote: Regardless of their nationality, persons who come to Switzerland by virtue of family reunification (their spouse as well as the children who are under the age of 21 or receive support) have the right to work anywhere in Switzerland and in the branch of their choice. They may also work in a self-employed capacity.

rows.fact_text: Residence permits issued to family members have the same duration of validity as the permit of the primary EU/EFTA citizen (main entitled person). The family member's right to stay is a derived right contingent on the primary person's right to stay. If the primary person leaves Switzerland or loses their permit, family members' permits are affected.
rows.evidence_quote: residence permits issued to family members have the same duration of validity as that of the original applicant (main entitled person).

rows.fact_text: Children of EU/EFTA nationals who legally reside in Switzerland (employed or inactive) may enrol in general education and vocational education and training under the same conditions as children of Swiss citizens. Children's residence permits derive from the primary applicant's permit and have the same validity duration.
rows.evidence_quote: The children of a foreign national who legally resides in Switzerland (regardless of whether he/she is economically active or inactive) may enrol in general education and vocational education and training under the same conditions as the children of Swiss citizens.

rows.fact_text: Third-country nationals may only work in Switzerland if they are highly qualified: managers, specialists, or other qualified workers. Must hold a degree from a university or institution of higher education plus professional work experience, or have specialist training with several years' experience. Must demonstrate professional and social adaptability, language skills, and appropriate age for long-term stays.
rows.evidence_quote: you may only do so if you are highly qualified, i.e. if you are a manager, specialist or other skilled professional. Workers should possess a degree from a university or an institution of higher education, as well as a number of years of professional work experience.

rows.fact_text: Admissions of non-EU/EFTA nationals are limited by annual quotas.
