The Federal Council determines maximum numbers annually in the Ordinance on Admission, Period of Stay and Employment (ASEO/VZAE). The Federal Council has kept quotas for third countries unchanged for 2024 and 2026. Quotas are distributed to cantons.
rows.evidence_quote: Admissions of non-EU and non-EFTA state nationals are limited. To this end, the Federal Council determines the maximum numbers in the Ordinance on Admission, Period of Stay and Employment (ASEO) on an annual basis.

rows.fact_text: Employers must prove priority was given to Swiss nationals, holders of C permits, and B permit holders before admitting a third-country national. Employers must demonstrate genuine recruitment efforts through regional employment centres (RAV) and the European Employment System (EURES), as well as sector-specific channels. Certain job vacancies in professions with unemployment at or above 5% must be registered with regional employment agencies.
rows.evidence_quote: Third-state nationals can be admitted only if it is not possible to recruit a person from Switzerland or from an EU/EFTA state. Employers must demonstrate genuine recruitment efforts through regional employment centers (RAV) and the European Employment System (EURES), plus sector-specific channels.

rows.fact_text: Salary, social security contributions, and employment terms for third-country workers must accord with local, professional, and sectoral conditions (conditions customary to the region, profession, and sector). Employment contracts must state the permit condition. Housing: suitable accommodation must be available for admitted workers.
rows.evidence_quote: Salary, social security contributions and employment terms for foreign workers must accord with local, professional and sectoral conditions. Foreign nationals may only be admitted in order to work if suitable accommodation for them is available.

rows.fact_text: Step 1: The employer submits application documents to the cantonal employment or immigration authority (Kantonales Amt für Wirtschaft und Arbeit / Office cantonal de l'emploi). Employees requiring a visa must also submit an application to the Swiss representation abroad covering their place of residence.
rows.evidence_quote: The employer submits the application documents to the cantonal employment or immigration authority. Employees requiring a visa must also submit an application to the Swiss representation abroad.

rows.fact_text: Step 2: Cantonal authority screens the application under FNIA and makes a preliminary decision. Approved applications are forwarded to SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) for national-level review. Step 3: SEM issues the official decision to all parties; employer pays a fee. SEM approval does not yet permit entry into Switzerland.
rows.evidence_quote: The competent cantonal authority screens applications on the basis of the Foreign Nationals and Integration Act and takes a preliminary decision. SEM reviews applications according to admission criteria that apply to the whole of Switzerland. The official decision goes to all involved parties and requires a fee paid by the employer.

rows.fact_text: Step 4: For applicants requiring a visa, the cantonal immigration authority issues electronic visa authorisation to the relevant Swiss representation abroad. The applicant collects the visa from the Swiss embassy/consulate in their country of residence. Step 5: Employee enters Switzerland and registers at commune of residence within 14 days. Work may not begin before registration.
rows.evidence_quote: The employee registers with the competent authority at their place of residence in Switzerland within 14 days of entering the country. The employee can only begin work after he or she has registered.

rows.fact_text: Standard processing time for a third-country work permit in Switzerland is generally 6 to 8 weeks for standard cases. Complex situations may take longer. The clock starts when the employer submits a complete application to the cantonal authority.
rows.evidence_quote: Generally six to eight weeks for standard cases, though complex situations may take longer.

rows.fact_text: Third-country nationals holding an L permit (short-term) may change jobs if they cannot continue with their current employer, but must remain within the same sector and same profession. B permit holders can generally change jobs without additional authorisation.
rows.evidence_quote: Short-term ('L') permit holders may change jobs if unable to continue with current employer, but must remain within the same sector as well as the same profession. 'B' permit holders generally can change without authorization.

rows.fact_text: Intra-company transfers of senior managers and essential specialists within international companies are exempt from the labour-market priority (precedence) rules. They are still subject to quotas and general FNIA admission requirements (qualifications, salary conditions, housing). Applies to operational transfers, not new hires.
rows.evidence_quote: The precedence rules do not apply to operational transfers for senior managers and essential specialists in international companies.

rows.fact_text: Individuals pursuing doctoral or post-doctoral research at a recognised or accredited Swiss higher education institution to develop a specialisation are exempt from the labour-market priority (precedence) rules. Must be continuing studies beyond a foundation degree at an accredited Swiss institution. The goal must be to ensure best possible development of science and technology in Switzerland.
rows.evidence_quote: Individuals who continue to study or pursue research work at a recognised or accredited Swiss higher education institution beyond their foundation degree, in order to develop a specialisation and thus ensure the best possible development of science and technology in Switzerland.

rows.fact_text: Third-country nationals may study in Switzerland with a student residence permit. Must show: (1) acceptance/admission to a state-recognised Swiss educational institution; (2) financial self-sufficiency for the full duration of studies; (3) health insurance. Permit issued for duration of studies with annual renewal required. Cannot start work until 6 months after studies begin.
rows.evidence_quote: Students must show admission to a state-recognized institution of learning, and that they can support themselves for the duration of their studies.

rows.fact_text: Third-country students in Switzerland may work a maximum of 15 hours per week outside of holidays, but only beginning no sooner than 6 months after the start of their course. An employer must submit an application. The university must confirm that the work is compatible with studies. Applies to universities and universities of applied sciences.
rows.evidence_quote: Beginning no sooner than six months after the start of their course, foreign students may work for a maximum of 15 hours a week outside of the holidays. The employer must submit an application and the university must confirm compatibility with studies.

rows.fact_text: Third-country student permit holders may apply for family reunification for spouse and dependent children (similar to EU/EFTA student route). Family members' right to work requires separate employer application. Student sponsors cannot bring dependent parents under the student route. Accommodation and financial self-sufficiency conditions apply.
rows.evidence_quote: Members of the family of holders of a short-term residence ('L') permit may be given permission to pursue gainful employment if an application is submitted by an employer and standard employment conditions are met.

rows.fact_text: Third-country nationals who have graduated from a recognised Swiss higher education institution (university or university of applied sciences) are entitled to a 6-month period from the end of their course to seek employment matching their qualifications. During this period they are exempt from the normal labour-market priority (precedence) rule evidence requirement. Must have completed the full course/training in Switzerland.
rows.evidence_quote: Third-country nationals who have graduated from a Swiss higher education institution have a six-month period from the end of their course or training in Switzerland in which to look for a job which matches their qualifications.

rows.fact_text: Third-country nationals admitted to work following graduation from a Swiss higher education institution do not need to provide evidence of their status under the precedence rule, provided there is a significant academic or economic interest in their employment. This exception applies only to degrees from recognised Swiss higher education institutions (universities and universities of applied sciences).
rows.evidence_quote: Foreign nationals can be admitted to work without having to provide evidence of their status under the precedence rule if there is a significant academic or economic interest in their employment. This rule applies only to degrees from recognised Swiss higher education institutions (universities and universities of applied sciences).

rows.fact_text: Third-country nationals holding a B permit (residence permit) may apply for family reunification for their spouse and children. The spouse of a B permit holder has the right to work without needing additional authorisation. Family members' permits have the same duration of validity as the primary permit holder's permit.
rows.evidence_quote: Spouses and children of holders of permanent residence permits have the right to work, without needing to go through any additional authorisation procedure.

rows.fact_text: Third-country nationals holding an L permit (short-term, under 12 months) may have their family members apply for employment authorisation, but only via employer application. Family members' work permission is not automatic — an employer must apply, and standard employment conditions (salary, qualifications) must be met. No standalone right to work for spouse of L permit holder.
rows.evidence_quote: Members of the family of holders of a short-term residence ('L') permit may be given permission to pursue gainful employment if an application is submitted by an employer and the rules on pay and working conditions, as well as personal qualifications, are satisfied.

rows.fact_text: Family reunification for third-country nationals is governed by the Foreign Nationals and Integration Act (FNIA) and is stricter than the EU/EFTA AFMP route. Conditions include: adequate financial means, suitable housing, and in some cases integration criteria. Detailed requirements are set in FNIA directives (available in German, French, Italian only). Canton of residence processes applications.
rows.evidence_quote: Family members of Swiss nationals and those holding residence permits do not need to go through an additional permit process to become self-employed or take up employment. Family members of people holding a short-term permit do require a permit.

rows.fact_text: Since 1 January 2021, UK nationals are classified as third-country nationals for Swiss immigration purposes. The Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (AFMP) between Switzerland and the EU no longer applies to the UK. New UK arrivals must apply for a permit from the cantonal immigration and labour market authorities prior to taking up employment, under FNIA rules.
rows.evidence_quote: The Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (AFMP) between Switzerland and the EU no longer applies with the UK from 1 January 2021. UK nationals coming to Switzerland to work from 1 January 2021 are third-country nationals. They must apply for a permit from the cantonal immigration and labour market authorities prior to taking up employment.

rows.fact_text: UK nationals who were residing in Switzerland before 31 December 2020 retain acquired rights under a bilateral agreement signed 25 February 2019. They keep the rights acquired up to 31 December 2020 based on the AFMP. Family reunification remains possible for this group after 2021. UK nationals arriving after 31 December 2020 are NOT covered by the acquired rights agreement.
rows.evidence_quote: Switzerland and the UK signed an agreement on 25 February 2019 on the acquired rights of their citizens...allows Swiss and UK nationals to keep the rights they acquired up to 31 December 2020 based on the AFMP. UK nationals coming to live and work in Switzerland after 31 December 2020 are not covered by the agreement on acquired rights.

rows.fact_text: A temporary UK-Switzerland Services Mobility Agreement (SMA), signed 14 December 2020, provides certain short-term service-provision rights for UK nationals in Switzerland. This covers specific categories of cross-border service providers and may allow work without a full permit for qualifying service categories. Separate from the standard third-country quota work permit route.
rows.evidence_quote: Temporary UK-Switzerland Services Mobility Agreement, SMA, signed on 14 December 2020.

rows.fact_text: All foreign nationals (EU/EFTA and third-country) must register at the commune (Einwohnerkontrolle / contrôle des habitants / controllo degli abitanti) of their place of residence within 14 days of arrival. EU/EFTA nationals must register before taking up work. Third-country nationals may not start work until registration is complete. This is where permit applications are submitted.
rows.evidence_quote: Within 14 days of their arrival and before actually taking up work, nationals of EU/EFTA states have to register with the local authorities of the commune in which they are residing and apply for a residence permit.

rows.fact_text: Third-country nationals must also register at their commune of residence within 14 days of entering Switzerland. The registration is mandatory before work commences. The cantonal migration office issues the formal residence permit card after registration. Moving to a new canton requires re-registration with the new commune.
rows.evidence_quote: The employee registers with the competent authority at their place of residence in Switzerland within 14 days of entering the country. The employee can only begin work after he or she has registered.

rows.fact_text: Swiss residence permits (L, B, C) are valid for the whole of Switzerland. Permit holders who relocate to a new canton must register with the new commune's authorities but do not need to obtain a new permit. The permit itself does not need to be reissued when changing cantons.
rows.evidence_quote: Permits are valid for the whole of Switzerland so residents need not obtain new permits when relocating, though they must register with the authorities of the new canton.

rows.fact_text: All persons taking up residence in Switzerland for more than 3 months are required by law to take out health insurance with a Swiss health insurance company (Krankenkasse) under the Health Insurance Act (KVG/LAMal). This obligation applies to EU/EFTA and third-country nationals alike. Non-compliance results in the canton assigning an insurer.
rows.evidence_quote: If you take up residence in Switzerland for more than 3 months, you are required by law to take out a health insurance with a Swiss health insurance company.

rows.fact_text: The mandatory health insurance requirement applies equally to third-country nationals residing in Switzerland for more than 3 months. For non-employed EU/EFTA nationals seeking a B permit without gainful activity, proof of adequate health and accident insurance is required to obtain the permit.
rows.evidence_quote: Nationals from all EU/EFTA member states without gainful employment are entitled to a B permit if they can prove they have sufficient financial means and adequate health and accident insurance.

rows.fact_text: All employees in Switzerland must be registered with AHV (Alters- und Hinterlassenenversicherung — Old-Age and Survivors Insurance). The employer registers the employee and deducts AHV contributions (approximately 5.3% from the employee, matched by the employer) from the salary. Registration occurs when employment begins. Applies to all nationalities.
rows.evidence_quote: Salary, social security contributions and employment terms for foreign workers must accord with local, professional and sectoral conditions.

rows.fact_text: Self-employed persons in Switzerland must register directly with the cantonal AHV compensation fund (Ausgleichskasse/Caisse de compensation) in their canton of residence. They pay both the employee and employer portions of AHV contributions (approximately 10.6% combined). Registration must occur when self-employment begins.
rows.evidence_quote: Generally, they shall receive the same tax and social benefits as Swiss citizens.

rows.fact_text: After commune registration and permit application, the cantonal migration office issues a biometric residence permit card. For third-country nationals, the card contains a microchip with two digital fingerprints and a facial image. For EU/EFTA nationals, the card is in credit-card format without a chip (since November 2019). Biometric data storage lasts 5 years.
rows.evidence_quote: The card contains a microchip with biometric data: two digital fingerprints and a facial image. The canton of residence handles applications and biometric data collection. A single company produces permits centrally, then delivers them through standard channels.

rows.fact_text: Residence permit fees cover application processing, issuance of the residence permit card, and (for third-country nationals) capture of biometric data. Specific fee amounts vary by canton. For third-country work permits, the employer pays a fee associated with the SEM decision. Cantonal fees are additional.
rows.evidence_quote: Residence permit fees cover application processing, issuance of residence permit and capture of biometric data.

rows.fact_text: Third-country nationals seeking self-employment in Switzerland must demonstrate that their self-employment will have a lasting positive impact on the Swiss labour market (overall economic interest). Required documentation includes: a comprehensive business plan, market analysis, workforce projections, and commercial registration details. Subject to quota and FNIA admission framework. Much stricter than EU/EFTA self-employment path.
rows.evidence_quote: You must demonstrate that self-employment will have a lasting positive impact on the Swiss labour market (overall economic interest). Applications require comprehensive documentation including business plans and market analyses.

rows.fact_text: The Young Professionals program (work permit for career development) is available to nationals of 15 specific countries including USA. Other common origin countries in scope NOT covered: India, China, Brazil, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Serbia, Sri Lanka, Eritrea, Turkey. Max permit duration: 18 months. Must work in learned profession. Part-time and self-employment not permitted.
rows.evidence_quote: Switzerland offers work permit agreements for young professionals from 15 eligible countries: Argentina, Australia, Canada, Chile, Indonesia, Japan, Monaco, New Zealand, Philippines, Russia, San Marino, South Africa, Tunisia, Ukraine, and the USA. Maximum 18-month work permits are available.

rows.fact_text: EU/EFTA nationals exercising free movement rights in Switzerland are NOT subject to a labour-market priority test. Employers do not need to prove that no Swiss or EU/EFTA national is available. This contrasts with the third-country route where employers must demonstrate that no suitable Swiss or EU/EFTA person could fill the vacancy.
rows.evidence_quote: only a limited number of workers admitted from non-EU/EFTA States, primarily management level employees, specialists and other qualified employees. Employers must prove there is no suitable person to fill the job vacancy from Switzerland or from an EU/EFTA state.

rows.fact_text: The EU/EFTA B permit under the AFMP applies to nationals of all 27 EU member states plus EEA/EFTA states (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland). Key nationalities in scope: Germany, France, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Austria, Netherlands, Poland, Romania. The AFMP explicitly no longer applies to the UK since 1 January 2021.

rows.fact_text: EU Regulation 883/2004 applies. The employer must obtain an A1 Certificate (Portable Document A1) from the French social security authority (URSSAF/CPAM) BEFORE the employee starts work in Germany. The A1 confirms the employee remains covered under French social security and is exempt from German social security contributions. Without an A1 Certificate, the employee may be subject to double social security contributions in both countries, and the employer may face back-contribution claims from German authorities (Deutsche Rentenversicherung). The certificate must be carried by the employee at all times and shown to German inspectors on request.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Employee seconded from France to Germany for any period

rows.fact_text: Under EU Directive 96/71/EC (Posted Workers Directive) as amended by Directive 2018/957/EU, the French employer must submit a prior notification to the German customs authority via the online minimum wage notification portal (www.meldeportal-mindestlohn.de) BEFORE the employee begins work in Germany. This notification must include employer details, the employee's name and role, assignment location, start and end dates, and a local contact person. Notification cannot be submitted by fax; it must be done online. Failure to notify is a regulatory offence under the MiLoMeldV and can result in fines of up to EUR 30,000.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Employee posted from France to perform work in Germany under the Posted Workers Directive

rows.fact_text: Germany's Minimum Wage Act (Mindestlohngesetz, MiLoG) requires all employers — including foreign employers — to pay employees working in Germany at least the German statutory minimum wage (currently EUR 12.82/hour as of January 2025; rising to EUR 14.60/hour from January 2027). The employer must also register with the German tax authority (Finanzamt) to obtain a German tax number (Steuernummer) for wage tax (Lohnsteuer) purposes and must file monthly Lohnsteuer-Anmeldungen via the ELSTER portal. The employer must also report each employee to the social security clearing house (DEÜV/A-Meldung) before the first paycheck. Failure to comply with minimum wage rules can result in fines of up to EUR 500,000.

applies_to.trigger_condition: French employer pays salary to employee working in Germany

rows.fact_text: If a French company's employee works in Germany in a way that creates a 'permanent establishment' (PE) under Article 5 of the France-Germany Double Taxation Treaty (signed 1959, last amended 2015), the French company may become subject to German corporate income tax on profits attributable to that PE. PE risk is triggered by: maintaining a fixed place of business in Germany (e.g. a dedicated office or desk), having an employee who habitually concludes contracts on behalf of the French employer, or assignment exceeding 12 months. Employers must conduct a PE risk assessment before any assignment and document that the employee does not exercise 'entrepreneurial functions' in Germany.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Employee works in Germany from a fixed or recurring location or acts with authority to conclude contracts on behalf of the French employer

rows.fact_text: Under the France-Germany Double Taxation Treaty, employment income is taxed where the work is physically performed (the 'work state' rule). If an employee works partly in France and partly in Germany, income must be apportioned. German wage tax (Lohnsteuer) applies to the German workdays from day one — there is no 183-day de minimis exemption for employees whose employer is a French resident company with a German PE. Since January 2025, Germany's approach to the taxation of French resident employees of French companies has created increased risk of double taxation for cross-border workers. Employers must track German workdays precisely and may need to operate German shadow payroll.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Employee is a French tax resident working in Germany; income allocation between France and Germany must be determined

rows.fact_text: While an A1 Certificate exempts the employee from German social security contributions, the French employer must continue paying French social charges (cotisations sociales) in France throughout the secondment, including contributions to URSSAF (health, family, old-age, unemployment). The employer also remains subject to French payroll taxes such as the taxe d'apprentissage and the formation professionnelle. These ongoing French social charge obligations are frequently missed by HR teams who assume that posting an employee to Germany suspends all French obligations. Failure to continue French contributions invalidates the A1 coverage and can result in retroactive liability in both countries.

applies_to.trigger_condition: French employee holds valid A1 certificate while seconded to Germany

rows.fact_text: The German Act on Temporary Agency Work (Arbeitnehmerüberlassungsgesetz, AÜG) applies where a French employer 'lends' an employee to a German user company. In this scenario, the French employer must hold a German AÜG licence issued by the Federal Employment Agency (Bundesagentur für Arbeit). Without an AÜG licence, the arrangement is illegal under German law and the German user company may be deemed the employee's legal employer. The maximum permissible lending period is 18 months. Inter-group secondments where the employee continues performing work exclusively for the French parent's German operations may be exempt, but the distinction is fact-specific and legal advice is required.

applies_to.trigger_condition: French employer lends or assigns an employee to a German third-party company (not an intra-group secondment to the French entity's own German operations)

rows.fact_text: French nationals have the right to work in Germany under EU freedom of movement (Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, Article 45). No work permit or visa is required. However, if the assignment exceeds 3 months, the employee must register with the local German registration office (Einwohnermeldeamt) within 14 days of taking up residence. The employer should also verify whether the employee needs to register for German health insurance locally if the A1 is not in place. For non-EU nationals who are employees of the French employer and are being seconded to Germany, separate work permit rules apply.

applies_to.trigger_condition: French citizen employee seconded to Germany (EU freedom of movement applies)

rows.fact_text: Although both France and Germany are EU member states and GDPR applies in both, HR data transfers between the two countries must comply with GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679). Employers must have a lawful basis for processing (typically performance of employment contract or compliance with legal obligation). German data protection law (BDSG 2018) adds additional restrictions: works councils (Betriebsrat) in Germany may have co-determination rights over HR monitoring systems; employee consent under BDSG must be genuinely voluntary. French employers must update their Records of Processing Activities (ROPA) to reflect the cross-border element. The French data protection authority (CNIL) and German Datenschutzbehörde both have audit powers.

applies_to.trigger_condition: French employer transfers employee HR data to German operations or German service providers

rows.fact_text: If a seconded employee's assignment to Germany lasts more than 12 months (extendable to 18 months under the AÜG with written justification), or if the employee becomes integrated into the German host company's operations, German employment law will apply in full. This includes German unfair dismissal protection (Kündigungsschutzgesetz, KSchG), which applies after 6 months of employment in companies with more than 10 employees. The employer must then comply with German notice periods, severance obligations, and works council consultation requirements. Converting a secondment to a local contract mid-assignment without proper legal structuring can trigger retroactive German employment law claims.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Secondment to Germany converts to or is reclassified as local German employment (assignment exceeds 12 months, or employee is integrated into German operations)

rows.fact_text: Indian nationals require a national work visa (D-Visa for employment) or EU Blue Card to work legally in Germany. As a non-EU national, the employee cannot work on a tourist or business visitor visa. The German employer (or the employer's German entity) must initiate the visa process by providing a signed employment contract, proof of qualification recognition, and an employer declaration (Erklärung zum Beschäftigungsverhältnis). The visa application is submitted at the German embassy in India, and processing typically takes 4–12 weeks. Working without a valid work permit is a criminal offence in Germany; the employer can face fines and reputational damage. The employee must not begin work until the visa is granted.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Indian national employee assigned to work in Germany

rows.fact_text: India and Germany have a bilateral Social Security Agreement (SSA) signed on 12 October 2011, in force since 1 May 2012. Under the SSA, an Indian employee seconded by an Indian employer to Germany for up to 5 years can obtain a Certificate of Coverage (CoC) from the Indian Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO). The CoC exempts the employee from mandatory German pension contributions (Deutsche Rentenversicherung Beitrag) and German unemployment insurance (Arbeitslosenversicherung) during the secondment. The CoC must be obtained from EPFO BEFORE the employee starts work in Germany. Without a CoC, the employer is required to make German pension and unemployment insurance contributions at the full German rate (employer share: approximately 9.3% pension + 1.3% unemployment). The Indian employer must remain the entity of record and continue making EPF contributions in India.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Indian employee seconded to Germany by Indian employer for a temporary assignment (up to 5 years)

rows.fact_text: For the Skilled Worker Visa (Fachkräftevisum) or EU Blue Card, the German employer must obtain formal recognition of the Indian employee's academic qualifications via the ANABIN database (maintained by the KMK — Kultusministerkonferenz) or via a formal equivalency assessment (Anerkennung). Degrees from Indian universities listed as H+ (equivalent) in ANABIN are accepted directly; others require a Statement of Comparability (Zeugnisbewertung) from the German Academic Exchange Service (KMK/ZAB). The employer's HR team must initiate this check as part of visa preparation — without qualification recognition, the visa will be refused. For regulated professions (engineering, medicine, law), additional professional recognition from the relevant Kammer (chamber) is required.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Indian employee applying for skilled worker visa or EU Blue Card for Germany

rows.fact_text: Any employer — including a foreign (Indian) employer — whose employee works in Germany and is subject to German income tax must register with the German tax authority (Finanzamt) for wage tax (Lohnsteuer) purposes and run German payroll. The employer must obtain a German tax identification number (Steuernummer) and file monthly Lohnsteuer-Anmeldungen electronically via the ELSTER portal. German income tax (Einkommensteuer) is due from the first day of German-source employment; there is no 183-day grace period where the employer is the foreign entity but the employee reports to German operations. Failure to register and withhold can result in the Finanzamt assessing back taxes plus interest against both the employer and employee.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Indian employer sends employee to Germany; German income tax withholding obligations arise

rows.fact_text: The India-Germany Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) governs which country may tax the employee's salary. Under Article 15 (employment income), Germany has primary taxing rights on salary attributable to work performed in Germany. The Indian employer may also be subject to Indian withholding obligations on the portion of salary taxable in India. If the Indian employer does not have a German PE, and the employee's stay is less than 183 days in a 12-month period, India retains taxing rights only if the employer is NOT a German resident AND the cost is not borne by a German PE. In practice, most employer-paid secondments exceeding 183 days trigger full German taxation. The employer must also assess PE risk if the employee habitually exercises authority to conclude contracts in Germany on behalf of the Indian company.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Indian employee works in Germany; India-Germany DTT applies to allocate taxation rights

rows.fact_text: Indian nationals may enter Germany visa-free or on a Schengen short-stay visa (C-Visa) for up to 90 days for business visitor activities (attending meetings, negotiating contracts, training). However, any productive work — including providing professional services or technical assistance — on a short-stay visa or as a tourist is prohibited and constitutes illegal employment. The employer must ensure the employee has a valid national work visa (D-Visa) or EU Blue Card before commencing any work activity. The 90-day Schengen rule is strictly enforced; overstays trigger entry bans and can affect future visa applications for the employee and create enforcement risk for the employer.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Indian employee enters Germany to begin work preparations or attend meetings before visa is issued

rows.fact_text: A seconded Indian employee remains employed by the Indian entity and retains their Indian employment contract. A locally hired employee in Germany is subject to full German employment law from day one, including the German Civil Code (BGB), Kündigungsschutzgesetz (KSchG) for unfair dismissal protection, the German Working Time Act (ArbZG), and Works Constitution Act (BetrVG) for co-determination. The compliance obligations differ substantially: a secondment requires Indian contract maintenance, A1/CoC coverage, and German posted-worker notifications; a local hire requires German employment contract, German payroll, and German statutory benefits. Misclassifying a local hire as a secondment to avoid German employment law creates legal exposure for both entities.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Employer assigns Indian employee to Germany under secondment arrangement vs. hiring locally

rows.fact_text: Under the German Skilled Immigration Act (Fachkräfteeinwanderungsgesetz), the German employer must submit an Erklärung zum Beschäftigungsverhältnis (declaration of employment conditions) as part of the visa application package. This declaration confirms: the employment terms meet German statutory minimums, the role is classified in an eligible occupation, and the salary meets the minimum threshold for the visa category (EU Blue Card threshold: EUR 43,800/year for standard roles; EUR 34,056 for shortage occupations as of 2024). The employer must also confirm that no equivalent EU/EEA candidate was available (for certain visa types). This employer declaration is mandatory — without it, the German embassy cannot process the visa application.

applies_to.trigger_condition: German employer submitting work permit application for Indian skilled worker

rows.fact_text: If the Indian employer fails to obtain an EPFO Certificate of Coverage (CoC) before the employee commences work in Germany, the employee and employer will be liable for mandatory German pension contributions (Deutsche Rentenversicherung) at the full German rate (employer: 9.3%, employee: 9.3% of gross salary, as of 2024) AND the Indian employer must continue making EPF contributions in India (employer: 12% of basic salary). This creates genuine double pension contribution costs that can increase total employment cost by 18–24% for the German assignment period. The CoC must be obtained from EPFO's International Workers Division; applications typically take 15–30 working days. Late applications cannot be backdated.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Indian employee works in Germany without Certificate of Coverage (CoC) from EPFO

rows.fact_text: Foreign companies providing services in Germany through posted workers must comply with the German Posted Workers Act (Arbeitnehmer-Entsendegesetz, AEntG). The employer must register with the German customs authority and submit a posting notification via the online minimum wage portal (www.meldeportal-mindestlohn.de) BEFORE the employee starts work. For IT and professional services assignments, minimum pay requirements under the AEntG and MiLoG apply. The employer must also maintain and produce on demand records of working hours, pay slips, and the employment contract (in German) for the duration of the assignment and for 2 years afterward. German customs and labour authorities (Zoll) conduct random inspections; non-compliance fines can reach EUR 500,000.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Indian company sends employee to work at a German client or third-party location

rows.fact_text: Following Brexit (effective 31 December 2020), US nationals and all non-UK/non-Irish nationals require a Skilled Worker Visa to work in the UK. The employer MUST be a licensed UK visa sponsor (approved by the Home Office) BEFORE the employee can apply for a visa. Without a sponsor licence, no Certificate of Sponsorship can be issued and the employee cannot legally work in the UK. The employer must check their sponsor licence status and apply if not already licensed. The Home Office may conduct a pre-licence audit of the employer's HR systems and compliance controls. Employing someone without the right to work in the UK can result in a civil penalty of up to GBP 60,000 per illegal worker (as of 2024) and criminal prosecution.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US employer sends an American or non-UK national employee to work in the UK post-Brexit

rows.fact_text: To sponsor a Skilled Worker, the employer must hold a valid UK Sponsor Licence issued by the Home Office. Applying for a sponsor licence requires: demonstrating a genuine need for the role, having compliant HR systems to track sponsored workers' attendance and visa status, appointing an Authorising Officer and Level 1 User in the Sponsorship Management System (SMS), and paying an application fee (GBP 536 for small employers; GBP 1,476 for large employers). Processing typically takes 8+ weeks (20 working days standard; 5 working days for priority service at additional cost). The employer must not assign a Certificate of Sponsorship until the licence is granted. Planning should begin at least 10–12 weeks before the intended start date.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US employer has not previously sponsored overseas workers in the UK

rows.fact_text: Once the employer holds a sponsor licence, they must assign a Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS) to the employee. A CoS is an electronic record (not a physical document) created in the Sponsorship Management System (SMS). The CoS must include: the job title and SOC code, the salary, the start date, and the assignment location. The employee uses the CoS reference number in their visa application. A defined CoS is required for out-of-country applicants; an undefined CoS for in-country applicants. The employer pays a CoS assignment fee (GBP 239 per CoS). The employer also becomes responsible for monitoring the worker's immigration status, reporting changes to the Home Office, and maintaining records for 5 years. Failure to fulfil sponsor duties can result in licence suspension or revocation.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK licensed sponsor employer assigning a worker under a Skilled Worker visa

rows.fact_text: From the employee's first day of work in the UK, the employer must operate UK PAYE (Pay As You Earn) payroll. This requires registering with HMRC as an employer, obtaining an Employer Reference Number (ERN/PAYE reference), and running a Real Time Information (RTI) payroll each pay period. The employer must deduct UK income tax and employee National Insurance contributions (NICs) from the employee's pay and pay employer NICs (13.8% on earnings above the secondary threshold). PAYE submissions must be made to HMRC on or before each payday. UK payroll obligations exist even if the employee remains nominally employed by the US entity — a 'shadow payroll' arrangement may be required if the employee continues on US payroll. Failure to register and operate PAYE results in HMRC penalties and interest.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US company employs or seconds a worker to the UK who performs work in the UK

rows.fact_text: The US and UK have a bilateral Totalization Agreement (in force since 1985) that prevents dual social security taxation. Under the Agreement, a US employer that temporarily sends an employee to the UK can retain the employee under US Social Security (FICA) coverage for up to 5 years by obtaining a US Certificate of Coverage from the Social Security Administration (SSA). Without this certificate, the employee and employer are liable for UK National Insurance contributions (NICs) in addition to US FICA taxes. The US employer must apply for the certificate from the SSA before the UK assignment begins. The certificate should be kept on file; a copy is sent to HMRC. Failure to obtain the certificate results in mandatory UK NIC liability retroactively from the first day of UK work.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US employer sends employee to the UK without obtaining a US Certificate of Coverage under the US-UK Totalization Agreement

rows.fact_text: The US-UK Double Taxation Convention (DTC) allocates taxing rights on employment income. The UK generally has the right to tax UK-source employment income from day one. The US taxes its citizens and residents on worldwide income regardless of where they live. This means a US citizen working in the UK is subject to both UK income tax (via PAYE) and US federal income tax. The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE) (Form 2555) and Foreign Tax Credit (FTC) mitigate but do not eliminate double taxation. The employer must ensure the employee is enrolled in correct payroll tax treatment in both countries, understand the residency tie-breaker rules in Article 4 of the DTC, and consider whether to offer tax equalisation or tax protection as part of the assignment package. Tax gross-up errors are a leading cause of cost overruns on US-UK assignments.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US employee assigned to the UK; double taxation risk under US-UK tax treaty

rows.fact_text: The UK Off-Payroll Working Rules (IR35), codified in the Income Tax (Earnings and Pensions) Act 2003 and reformed from April 2021, apply where a worker provides services through an intermediary (e.g. a personal service company) to a medium or large UK client/end-user. The end-user (which may be the UK operation of the US company) must conduct an employment status determination (Status Determination Statement, SDS) using HMRC's CEST tool. If the worker would be an employee if engaged directly, the deemed employer must deduct PAYE and employer NICs. Incorrect IR35 determinations expose the deemed employer to underpaid tax, NIC, interest and penalties. Small UK clients are exempt but must still assess status. This commonly affects US companies using UK contractor relationships without proper IR35 assessment.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US company engages an individual in the UK through a personal service company (PSC) or as an independent contractor rather than employee

rows.fact_text: UK employers are legally required to carry out a Right to Work check on every worker BEFORE they start working. The check must confirm the worker has the legal right to work in the UK. Acceptable methods include: checking original physical documents from the Home Office's list (e.g. BRP, passport with visa endorsement), using the Home Office online checking service (for those with a share code), or using an Identity Document Validation Technology (IDVT) provider for British/Irish nationals. The check must be completed before the first day of work — retrospective checks do not provide a statutory excuse. The employer must keep a copy of evidence for 2 years after the employment ends. Failure to conduct a valid Right to Work check results in a civil penalty of up to GBP 60,000 per illegal worker.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Employer hires or seconds any worker to the UK, regardless of nationality

rows.fact_text: Even if a US-UK Totalization Agreement Certificate of Coverage is obtained (exempting the employee from UK NICs), the US employer must continue withholding US FICA taxes (Social Security: 6.2% employee + 6.2% employer; Medicare: 1.45% + 1.45%) on the US-source portion of the employee's earnings. The IRS requires employers to use Revenue Procedures 80-56 and 84-54 in conjunction with the Totalization Agreement to establish the exemption. US employers must also consider the Additional Medicare Tax (0.9%) for high earners. Common errors include ceasing FICA withholding entirely when the employee moves to the UK, or failing to apply the correct totalization procedures in FICA filings.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US employer maintains employee under US payroll and FICA while the employee works in the UK

rows.fact_text: The UK Modern Slavery Act 2015 requires organisations with an annual global turnover of GBP 36 million or more and doing business in the UK to publish an annual Slavery and Human Trafficking Transparency Statement approved by their Board of Directors and signed by a director. The statement must describe the steps taken to ensure modern slavery is not present in the business or supply chain. This applies to US parent companies with UK operations. The statement must be published on the company website with a prominent link on the homepage. Failure to publish a statement (or publishing an inadequate one) can result in enforcement action by the UK Single Enforcement Body (from 2025). For employers bringing workers into the UK from overseas, the statement should address recruitment practices and visa/relocation cost policies to prevent debt bondage.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US company with UK operations has a global annual turnover of GBP 36 million or more and employs UK workers

rows.fact_text: Post-Brexit, UK nationals are no longer covered by EU Regulation 883/2004 for new assignments. No bilateral social security agreement existed between UK and Germany until none was concluded post-Brexit (the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement covers only limited coordination for existing cross-border workers predating 1 January 2021). A UK employer sending a new employee to Germany from 2021 onwards faces potential double social security contributions: German statutory contributions (Sozialversicherung) apply from day one of German employment, and UK NI may also apply under domestic rules if the employer continues UK payroll. Employers must take specialist advice before the assignment commences to determine the applicable legislation and apply for any available certificate of coverage via HMRC.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employee seconded or relocated to Germany (post-Brexit, commenced on or after 1 January 2021)

rows.fact_text: Since 1 January 2021, UK nationals no longer benefit from EU free movement rights. To work in Germany, a UK national must obtain a German residence and work permit before starting employment. The primary route for skilled employees is the Aufenthaltserlaubnis zur Beschäftigung (residence permit for employment) or the EU Blue Card for high earners, governed by the Fachkräfteeinwanderungsgesetz (Skilled Immigration Act). The employer bears the obligation to ensure the employee has the correct immigration status before work commences; employing without a valid permit can result in substantial fines for the employer. Processing times at the German Ausländerbehörde can exceed 8-12 weeks, and employers should apply well in advance. From June 2024, the Skilled Immigration Act final phase enables recognition of non-EU qualifications, which may benefit UK workers seeking equivalency.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK national taking up employment in Germany for any duration post-Brexit

rows.fact_text: A UK driving licence is only valid in Germany for the first 6 months after the employee establishes normal residence. After that period, the UK licence ceases to be legally recognised for driving in Germany. The employee must exchange the UK licence for a German licence at the local Bürgeramt; no driving test is required for the exchange, but the process requires an appointment and takes several weeks. Employers with employees who drive as part of their job (company vehicles, client visits) must track this 6-month deadline. Driving beyond 6 months on an unexchanged UK licence constitutes driving without a valid licence under German law and may invalidate company vehicle insurance.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employee taking up residence in Germany and requiring a driving licence for work

rows.fact_text: UK employees who cease paying UK National Insurance contributions during a German assignment accumulate gaps in their UK state pension entitlement. Unlike citizens covered by EU social security coordination (Regulation 883/2004), post-2021 new assignees to Germany cannot rely on aggregation of UK and German contribution periods for UK state pension purposes. Employers should inform employees of the option to pay voluntary Class 2 or Class 3 UK NI contributions to preserve state pension entitlement during the German posting. There is also a risk that German pension contributions (Deutsche Rentenversicherung) paid during the posting are not portable back to the UK state pension given the absence of a bilateral agreement, creating a pension efficiency gap.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employee on long-term assignment or permanent relocation to Germany

rows.fact_text: Germany implements the EU Posted Workers Directive (Directive 96/71/EC as amended by Directive 2018/957/EU). Foreign employers posting workers to Germany must submit a mandatory notification via the German Zoll (customs authority) online portal (www.meldeportal-mindestlohn.de) before the posting commences. The notification must include worker details, posting duration, place of work, and the host employer contact. German minimum wage (Mindestlohn) and sector-specific collectively agreed wages apply to posted workers from day one. The Zollamt (customs office) enforces compliance via on-site inspections. Failure to notify or to pay minimum wage can result in fines of up to €500,000. UK employers are third-country employers under the Arbeitnehmer-Entsendegesetz (Posted Workers Act) after Brexit and must comply regardless of assignment length.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employer posting employees to perform services or work in Germany (temporary basis)

rows.fact_text: An employer without a German registered entity (GmbH, branch, or permanent establishment) that has an employee habitually working in Germany will typically create a taxable presence (permanent establishment) and must register with the German Finanzamt for wage tax (Lohnsteuer) purposes. The employer is obliged to withhold German income tax and social security contributions from the first day of German employment. If the UK employer does not establish a German payroll, it must engage a licensed Employer of Record (EOR) in Germany. Operating without proper German payroll registration is a significant compliance risk, including retroactive tax assessments, penalties, and interest. DATEV or Lohnabrechnung providers can handle German payroll; a Steuerberater (tax adviser) is typically required.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employer with employee working in Germany without a German legal entity

rows.fact_text: Following Brexit, the UK became a 'third country' for EU GDPR purposes. Transfers of personal data from Germany (or any EU/EEA country) to the UK require a legal transfer mechanism under GDPR Article 46. The European Commission granted an adequacy decision for the UK in June 2021 (initially for 4 years, currently under review for extension). HR data transfers — payslips, performance reviews, health data — from German employees to UK head office systems therefore currently rely on this adequacy decision. Employers must monitor the adequacy decision's status; if it lapses or is revoked, standard contractual clauses (SCCs) or binding corporate rules (BCRs) must be in place as fallback. The German data protection authority (Datenschutzkonferenz) applies additional scrutiny to cross-border transfers.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employer transferring personal data of German-based employees to UK systems or vice versa

rows.fact_text: Post-Brexit, UK professional qualifications are no longer automatically recognised under EU Directive 2005/36/EC on the recognition of professional qualifications. UK-qualified professionals wishing to practice regulated professions in Germany (e.g. Rechtsanwalt, Arzt, Ingenieur in regulated fields) must apply for individual recognition via the relevant German Kammer (professional chamber) or competent authority. The Anerkennungsberatung (recognition advisory service) at 'Anerkennung in Deutschland' provides guidance. Recognition processes can take 3-12 months and may require aptitude tests or supervised practice periods. UK employers must not assume German clients or counterparties will accept UK professional credentials at face value for legally-regulated work.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employee with regulated professional qualification (e.g. lawyer, engineer, doctor, accountant) working in Germany

rows.fact_text: Pre-Brexit, UK employers used the A1 certificate to confirm that an employee remained subject to UK NI and was therefore exempt from host-country social security. Post-Brexit, A1 certificates are no longer available to UK workers newly posted to EU member states (they remain available only for workers covered by the EU Withdrawal Agreement who were in cross-border situations before 1 January 2021). For new assignments to Germany from 2021 onwards, UK employers must assess the applicable social security legislation under domestic UK and German rules without the benefit of an A1. HMRC can issue a certificate of coverage under the limited provisions of the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement, but this only applies where the TCA coordination provisions apply. Employers should seek bespoke advice from a social security specialist for each assignment.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employer seeking to confirm which social security regime applies for a UK employee in Germany

rows.fact_text: Any foreign national (including US citizens) working in Singapore requires a valid work pass. The Employment Pass (EP) is the appropriate pass for professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) earning at least SGD 5,600 per month (as of 2024; increases progressively with age, up to SGD 10,700 at age 45 and above). The employer must be a Singapore-registered entity or have a registered address in Singapore and must be an approved MOM sponsor. The employer submits the EP application online via the EP eService. Employing a foreign national without a valid pass is a criminal offence under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act (EFMA), punishable by fines and imprisonment. The employer must also cancel the EP within one week of the employee ceasing employment.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US employer sending an employee to work in Singapore

rows.fact_text: The Fair Consideration Framework (FCF) requires employers with 10 or more employees to advertise the job vacancy on MyCareersFuture.sg for a minimum of 14 consecutive days before submitting an EP application, unless the role qualifies for an exemption. Exemptions include: the fixed monthly salary is SGD 22,500 or above; the employer has fewer than 10 employees; the posting duration is 1 month or less; or the role is an internal transfer. During the 14-day advertising period, the employer must not make a job offer to any candidate. The advertisement must accurately reflect the role, salary range, and vacancy count; the salary range cannot exceed double the minimum offered. MOM actively monitors compliance and can debar non-compliant employers from hiring foreign employees for up to 24 months. False declarations attract criminal prosecution under EFMA.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Singapore employer (with 10 or more employees) applying for an Employment Pass for a US hire

rows.fact_text: Employment Pass holders (foreign nationals) are explicitly exempt from Singapore's Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions. Employers must NOT deduct CPF from EP holders' salaries, and employers have no CPF employer contribution obligation for EP holders. A common compliance error is inadvertently including EP holders in a CPF payroll run. Conversely, US citizens working abroad remain subject to US FICA (Social Security and Medicare) taxes unless they can demonstrate exemption. The US-Singapore Totalization Agreement (entered into force 1 October 2009) prevents dual US and Singapore social security taxation. Under the agreement, a US employer should obtain a Certificate of US Coverage from the US Social Security Administration (SSA) to confirm the employee remains subject to US Social Security rather than Singapore's CPF. EP holders are outside CPF regardless, so the main risk is inadvertent FICA non-payment by US employers who wrongly assume overseas employment removes US FICA liability.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US employer with US citizen or Green Card holder employee working in Singapore on Employment Pass

rows.fact_text: The United States taxes its citizens and permanent residents on worldwide income regardless of where they live or work. A US employee seconded to Singapore must still file a US federal income tax return and report their Singapore-source income. To avoid double taxation, employees may claim either the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE) under IRC §911 (up to USD 126,500 in 2024) or the Foreign Tax Credit (FTC) under IRC §901 for Singapore income taxes paid. Employers with tax equalisation policies bear the obligation to calculate the tax cost carefully — an error in FEIE vs FTC election can result in significant unexpected US tax liability. Additionally, FBAR (FinCEN 114) filings are required if the employee holds Singapore bank accounts with aggregate balances exceeding USD 10,000.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US citizen or Green Card holder employee working in Singapore

rows.fact_text: Singapore levies income tax on income earned in or derived from Singapore. The residency status of the employee determines the applicable tax rate. An employee who is in Singapore for 183 days or more in a calendar year is treated as a tax resident and taxed at progressive resident rates (up to 24% for income above SGD 1 million). An employee present for fewer than 183 days is taxed at a flat non-resident rate (currently 15% on employment income, or progressive rates if higher). The employer is legally obligated to perform tax clearance (Form IR21) for foreign employees before they cease employment or leave Singapore, and must withhold any outstanding tax from the final salary. The IRAS Not-Ordinarily Resident (NOR) scheme may reduce Singapore tax for qualifying assignees who spend substantial time outside Singapore during their assignment.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Foreign employee (US national) working in Singapore on Employment Pass

rows.fact_text: Singapore's Employment Act (Cap. 91A) provides statutory protections for employees. The Act fully covers employees earning SGD 4,500 per month or below. For employees earning above SGD 4,500 per month (which includes most EP holders), Part IV protections (rest days, hours of work, overtime) do not apply, but the core provisions (salary payment, termination notice, annual leave, sick leave) still apply to non-workmen. Employers must ensure employment contracts comply with EA requirements regardless of EP holder status. Specific obligations include at least 7 days' annual leave in the first year (rising to 14 days), paid sick leave, and timely salary payment within 7 days of the salary period. US-style at-will employment is not recognised in Singapore; termination must comply with EA notice requirements.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US employer employing staff in Singapore under Employment Pass

rows.fact_text: Since 1 September 2023, all new Employment Pass applications (other than those with salary at or above SGD 22,500/month, which are auto-approved at Stage 1) must pass a two-stage assessment. Stage 1 is salary eligibility. Stage 2 is the Complementarity Assessment Framework (COMPASS), a points-based system scoring candidates across four foundational criteria: (1) salary relative to local PMET benchmark; (2) qualifications; (3) diversity (nationality concentration of employer's workforce); and (4) support for local employment (local PMET share). Candidates must score at least 40 points. Employers with high concentrations of a single nationality or low local PMET ratios will find EP applications harder to approve. HR teams must audit their workforce composition before submitting applications to avoid predictable COMPASS rejections.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Employer submitting Employment Pass application from September 2023 onwards

rows.fact_text: Singapore's National Service (NS) obligations apply to male Singapore Citizens and Second-Generation Permanent Residents (PRs). If a US national employee holds dual citizenship (US-Singapore) or Singapore PR status, they may have outstanding NS obligations that could affect their ability to remain in Singapore or re-enter Singapore for the duration of an assignment. Male Singapore Citizens must complete full-time NS (approximately 22-24 months) and are subject to in-camp training (ICT) for up to 40 days per year thereafter. Defaulting on NS obligations is a criminal offence. Employers should verify NS status for any US national who is also a Singapore Citizen or PR before planning a Singapore assignment, as unplanned disruptions to the assignment are a material HR risk.

applies_to.trigger_condition: US national employee who is also a Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident

rows.fact_text: Singapore operates a self-assessment tax system where employees file their own tax returns; however, employers have mandatory obligations. Employers must submit employee earnings information to IRAS annually (Form IR8A, due by 1 March each year) and, for employers participating in the Auto Inclusion Scheme (AIS), submit earnings data electronically so that it pre-populates employees' tax returns. Before a foreign employee ceases employment or departs Singapore, the employer must file Form IR21 (tax clearance) at least one month before the cessation date and withhold any balance of monies due to the employee until IRAS issues a tax clearance directive. Failure to file IR21 or to withhold salary makes the employer liable for any tax outstanding from the employee.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Singapore employer paying salary to foreign (EP holder) employee

rows.fact_text: Any UK employer wishing to sponsor a non-UK, non-Irish national (including Indian nationals) for employment in the UK must hold a valid Skilled Worker Sponsor Licence issued by UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI). Without a sponsor licence, the employer cannot issue a Certificate of Sponsorship and the employee cannot apply for a Skilled Worker visa. Applying for a sponsor licence takes approximately 8 weeks and requires the employer to demonstrate a genuine vacancy, HR systems capable of sponsor duties, and a UK legal presence. The licence application fee is £611 for small or charitable organisations and £1,682 for medium and large organisations. Employers should apply at least 10-12 weeks in advance of the intended start date to allow for processing and CoS issuance. Operating without a licence while employing sponsored workers is a criminal offence.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employer wishing to hire or second an Indian national into the UK

rows.fact_text: A Certificate of Sponsorship (CoS) is a unique electronic reference number assigned by the employer to a specific role for a specific worker. Each CoS is tied to the worker, the occupation code, the salary, and the employer. Employers must ensure the CoS accurately reflects the role and salary; discrepancies between the CoS and the actual employment terms are a common compliance failure that can result in visa refusal or revocation. The CoS must be assigned before the employee applies for the visa. Once a CoS is assigned, the worker has 3 months to make their visa application. Employers are responsible for notifying UKVI if the sponsored worker does not start, changes roles, or leaves employment. Failure to report changes within the required timeframes is a sponsor duty breach that can lead to licence downgrade or revocation.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employer with Sponsor Licence hiring an Indian national on Skilled Worker visa

rows.fact_text: Employers sponsoring a Skilled Worker must pay the Immigration Skills Charge (ISC) when assigning the Certificate of Sponsorship. The ISC is a mandatory levy payable by the employer (it is illegal to pass this cost to the sponsored worker). The rate is: £480 per year (£240 per additional 6-month period) for small or charitable sponsors; £1,320 per year (£660 per additional 6-month period) for medium and large sponsors. For a 5-year visa, the maximum liability is £2,400 (small) or £6,600 (large). The ISC must be paid in full at the time of CoS assignment, not in instalments. Failure to pay results in the worker's visa application being refused. Partial refunds are available if the worker leaves early or their visa is refused. SMEs frequently underestimate the total cost of sponsorship: CoS fee (£239–£525) + ISC + visa application fee + healthcare surcharge (paid by the employee) + sponsor licence fee amortised over assignments.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employer assigning a Certificate of Sponsorship for a Skilled Worker or Senior/Specialist Worker visa

rows.fact_text: The minimum salary threshold for the Skilled Worker visa is the higher of: (a) the general salary threshold (£41,700 per year as of July 2025, raised from £38,700 from April 2024); or (b) the 'going rate' for the specific occupation code (SOC code) as published by UKVI. Employers cannot pay below the going rate even if the employee agrees, and cannot pay different rates to sponsored workers vs comparable non-sponsored workers. New entrant rates (70% of the going rate, minimum £33,400) apply only to specific early-career criteria. Underpaying sponsored workers relative to the CoS salary or going rate is the most common sponsor compliance failure for SMEs and results in sponsor licence revocation. Employers must also note that salary increases must be updated on the CoS and notified to UKVI if the change in salary falls below the minimum threshold.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employer determining the salary to offer an Indian national on a Skilled Worker visa

rows.fact_text: UK employers have a statutory duty to check that every employee has the right to work in the UK before employment commences. For sponsored workers, the right to work check must be completed before the start date and repeated when the visa is extended or renewed. The check can be performed via the Home Office online service (share code provided by the worker) or by inspecting original documents. Since February 2024, civil penalties for employing illegal workers increased significantly: up to £45,000 per illegal worker for a first breach, and up to £60,000 for repeat breaches. For sponsored workers, employers must also retain copies of the right to work documents throughout employment and for 2 years after the employment ends. A failed or inadequate right to work check provides no statutory excuse; the employer remains liable for civil penalties even if the worker presented false documents, unless the employer used the online verification system.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employer employing any worker, including Indian nationals on Skilled Worker visas

rows.fact_text: UK employers must pay secondary Class 1 National Insurance contributions (employer NI) on earnings above the Secondary Threshold (£96 per week / £5,000 per year in 2024/25). The employer NI rate is 13.8% above the Secondary Threshold and applies from the first payroll run regardless of the employee's nationality or visa type. From April 2025, the employer NI rate increased to 15% and the Secondary Threshold was reduced to £5,000 per year. Employers must register with HMRC for PAYE before the employee starts work and must operate Real Time Information (RTI) submissions on or before each payment date. Failure to register or to pay employer NI on time attracts interest and penalties. Indian nationals on Skilled Worker visas have no exemption from UK employer NI.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employer adding an Indian national employee to UK payroll

rows.fact_text: The UK and India signed a National Insurance Double Contributions Convention (DCC) which entered into force on 15 July 2026. Prior to this date, there was no comprehensive bilateral social security agreement between the UK and India, creating a risk of double contributions: Indian Provident Fund (EPF) contributions on Indian earnings plus UK NI contributions on UK earnings. From 15 July 2026, employees sent temporarily from India to work in the UK (for up to 60 months) may remain subject to Indian social security (EPF/EPS) and be exempt from UK NI, provided they hold a certificate of coverage from India's EPFO. Conversely, UK employees sent to India on a temporary basis may continue paying UK NI and be exempt from Indian social security. HR teams must verify assignment start date relative to 15 July 2026 to determine whether the DCC exemption applies. For assignments straddling that date, transitional rules apply.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Indian national employed in UK, or UK employer with Indian-seconded employee from 15 July 2026

rows.fact_text: Indian university degrees and professional qualifications must be assessed for authenticity and comparability with UK standards when the role requires a regulated qualification or when UKVI uses the qualification as part of COMPASS scoring. UK NARIC (now UK ENIC) provides comparability statements for Indian qualifications. For regulated professions (doctors via GMC, nurses via NMC, accountants via ICAEW/ACCA/CIMA, solicitors via SRA), the relevant professional body must formally recognise the Indian qualification before the individual can practise. The process varies by profession: medical qualifications require an IELTS/OET test and PLAB examination; solicitors must pass the Solicitors Qualifying Examination (SQE). Employers who hire Indian nationals into regulated roles without checking professional recognition status may expose themselves to regulatory and professional liability.

applies_to.trigger_condition: Indian national with professional degree or regulated qualification seeking to work in a regulated UK profession

rows.fact_text: Holding a Skilled Worker Sponsor Licence creates ongoing compliance obligations ('sponsor duties') which are commonly underestimated by SMEs. Core duties include: (1) Record-keeping — retaining copies of all sponsored worker documents; (2) Reporting — notifying UKVI within 10 working days of specific events (e.g. absence without permission for 10 or more consecutive days, worker's salary falling below the CoS salary, change of job role or location); (3) Cooperation — allowing UKVI to conduct compliance visits with no notice; (4) Not assigning CoS to workers who do not meet the eligibility requirements. UKVI conducts routine audits of sponsors and can downgrade a licence from A-rating to B-rating (which prevents issuing new CoS) or revoke the licence entirely, rendering all sponsored workers immediately unlawfully employed. SME HR teams frequently miss the 10-working-day reporting window for salary changes or absences.

applies_to.trigger_condition: UK employer holding a Skilled Worker Sponsor Licence with Indian nationals on sponsored visas

Street address in Norway once housing is confirmed.
Bring a signed letter from the Norwegian employer confirming employment and salary.

rows.label_en: Norwegian tax residency does not end automatically on departure (10-year / 3-year rule)
rows.fact_text: Norwegian tax residency does NOT end simply because the employee has moved to France. Until cessation ('tax emigration') is established, the person keeps a global (worldwide) tax liability to Norway. Under skatteloven § 2-1 third paragraph, residence ends for a person taking permanent residence abroad only for the income year in which they show they spent no more than 61 days in Norway and that neither they nor close family (spouse, cohabitant, minor children) had a dwelling at their disposal in Norway. If total residence in Norway was 10 years or more before the departure year, residency can only end after the end of the third income year following the year of taking permanent residence abroad — and only if the 61-day and no-dwelling conditions are documented for each of those three years. This is a classic 'week-seven ambush': the employee can be doubly tax-resident for years without realising it.

rows.label_en: Norwegian exit tax (utflyttingsskatt) on latent gains when moving abroad
rows.fact_text: If the employee holds shares, fund units, share-savings accounts or similar assets with unrealised (latent) gains, moving abroad from Norway triggers Norwegian exit tax (utflyttingsskatt): the assets are taxed as if realised on the last day before tax residency ends or treaty residence shifts (skatteloven § 10-70). On emigration the charge applies only to the part of total net gains exceeding NOK 3 million. Payment can be deferred for up to 12 years — in yearly twelfths or in full at the end of the period with interest — with security required where there is a real recovery risk; the tax lapses for assets still held if the person becomes Norwegian tax resident again within 12 years. The rules were substantially reworked with effect from 2024 amendments, so whether and how it applies requires professional determination — an easily-missed cost that surfaces after the move.

rows.label_en: Determine applicable social security legislation under EEA Reg. 883/2004

So an employee who relocates to France and works there — even for a retained Norwegian employer — is in principle subject to FRENCH social security, unless the assignment qualifies as a temporary posting (A1 certificate, home-country coverage) or as multi-state activity (Art. 13). Practically: a French/EU national's right to work flows from the EEA Agreement and is confirmed by police registration in Norway; a non-EEA national needs a Norwegian residence permit from UDI, not an EU/Schengen work authorisation.

rows.official_guidance: Payroll reporting is a year-end task.
rows.actual_reality: The a-melding is a MONTHLY unified report (employment, salary, withholding) to the Tax Administration + NAV + SSB, due by the 5th of the month after the start/payment. Late or erroneous filing draws an enforcement fine, and the enterprise is identified by its org number — so reporting must be set up, with the org number in place, before the first paycheck.
rows.action_required: Stand up a-melding reporting (payroll system or direct) with the org number before the first pay run, and diarise the monthly 5th deadline.

rows.label_en: Preliminary withholding tax (forskuddstrekk) deducted from salary
rows.fact_text: The employer must, of its own initiative, deduct preliminary withholding tax (forskuddstrekk) from every salary payment in accordance with the employee's current electronic tax card (skattebetalingsloven § 5-4), and settle it with Skatteetaten; withholding is reported through the a-melding. If the employer has no access to the employee's tax-card information, the statutory default deduction is 50 % of the payment (§ 5-5 first paragraph). The withholding duty applies to whoever pays out the salary, including a foreign employer.
rows.evidence_quote: Arbeidsgiver plikter av eget tiltak å foreta forskuddstrekk i henhold til det til enhver tid gjeldende skattekortet og reglene i dette kapitlet. (§ 5-4 første ledd)
rows.source_version: Skattebetalingsloven (LOV-2005-06-17-67) § 5-4 / § 5-5, lovdata consolidated text — Sist endret LOV-2026-06-19-45

rows.actual_reality: The employer must deduct preliminary withholding (forskuddstrekk) from EVERY salary payment per the employee's electronic tax card and settle it with Skatteetaten. With no access to the tax card, the statutory default is 50% withholding. The duty applies even to a foreign employer.
rows.action_required: Complete the D-number → tax-card chain before the first run; without the tax card you must withhold 50%, so prioritise it.

rows.guidance: § 2-2-3 lists further alternative grounds for assigning a D-number (letters b to g). Only the tax-liability ground in letter a is quoted here, because it is the one this corridor relies on. The requisition procedure and the certified identity-document requirement are in § 2-2-4.
rows.fact_text: A D-number is the temporary Norwegian identification number for a person who does not meet the conditions for a fødselsnummer. It can be assigned to, among others, a person who is liable to tax in Norway or is in a business relationship with a Norwegian financial institution (folkeregisterforskriften § 2-2-3) — which is why it is needed before the employee can receive a tax card, be paid correctly, or open a bank account. It is requisitioned by an authority or financial institution with a need for it (for a worker, typically via the tax administration in the tax-card process), supported by a certified copy of the passport or equivalent identification (§ 2-2-4). HR should initiate this alongside relocation rather than waiting for the employee to arrive.
